stories.title: Lakers' Austin Reaves (heel bruise) to sit out vs. Suns
stories.summary: Los Angeles Lakers guard Austin Reaves will not play against the Phoenix Suns on Sunday because of a left heel bruise, the team announced.
stories.detailText: Los Angeles Lakers guard Austin Reaves will not play against the Phoenix Suns on Sunday because of a left heel bruise, the team announced. Lakers coach JJ Redick had previously said Reaves would be "day-to-day" while dealing with the injury, which he suffered in Wednesday's 123-112 road win over the Milwaukee Bucks while landing awkwardly after missing a contested fastbreak dunk attempt. When the doors opened for Lakers practice Saturday and reporters were let in, Reaves could be seen on the sidelines wearing slide sandals -- but without any wrap or boot on his left foot. Redick said that Reaves did not practice, staying off his feet to help the bruise heal. Reaves is averaging 24.7 points on 51.3% from the field, 40.9% from 3 and 91.5% from the foul line with 4.7 assists and 3.3 rebounds this season. L.A. (11-2) is tied with the San Antonio Spurs for the best record in the league, Sunday begins a stretch of three games in four days for the Lakers -- albeit against lesser opponents. After going on the road to play Phoenix (5-6), the Lakers host the Charlotte Hornets (4-8) on Tuesday and then the Utah Jazz (1-2) on Wednesday. Lakers backup guard Collin Sexton , who required stitches above his right eye after the Milwaukee game, is listed as questionable for Phoenix. Sexton practiced Saturday and told reporters he planned to play with goggles against the Suns, however. L.A. reserves Bronny James Jr. (illness) and Adou Thiero (left ankle sprain) are also listed as questionable and Lakers rookie Cameron Carr has been ruled out because of an illness.

stories.summary: The Philadelphia 76ers ruled out center Joel Embiid for Sunday's game against the Indiana Pacers with right foot plantar fascia management, the team announced Saturday.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA -- The Philadelphia 76ers ruled out center Joel Embiid for Sunday's game against the Indiana Pacers with right foot plantar fascia management, the team announced Saturday. Big men Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain) and Dominick Barlow (back) are also out. Barlow hasn't played this season, and coach Nick Nurse said Saturday that he is "progressing" but has no timeline for his return. LeBron James , who missed Thursday's win over the Toronto Raptors with sciatica and low back management, wasn't listed on the injury report. Without Embiid, Bona and Barlow, the Sixers will be significantly thin in the frontcourt. Tacko Fall , a two-way player, is the only active center on the roster. The Sixers will likely lean on James, Jabari Walker and Dean Wade to fill in the responsibilities at center. The Sixers are 1-1 without Embiid this season. In those games, James started the first at center -- a loss to Detroit -- and then Bona in a win against the Hornets. The game is the front end of a back-to-back; the Sixers will play the Nets in Brooklyn on Monday. Embiid and James haven't played both games of a back-to-back this season.

stories.title: While tied for NBA's best record, Lakers believe they can be better
stories.summary: JJ Redick and his coaching staff continue to point out the team's rebounding and defensive issues along with having too many turnovers.
stories.detailText: Lakers coach JJ Redick slaps hand with forward Ziaire Williams as he comes off the court during a timeout. (Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times) While rocketing toward the top of the league, the Lakers have been far from perfect. That’s good news to them. “A big thing that we talk with our players about a lot is being able to learn and get better and try to correct things even when you are winning,” coach JJ Redick said. The Lakers (11-2) have won seven consecutive games entering Sunday’s 1 p.m. PST matinee against the Suns (5-6) in Phoenix. Using a rare multiple-day break between games to audit their performances, coaches and analytics staffers showed slide presentations to players about both offensive and defensive flaws this week. The lectures left the team with one of the best records in the league feeling as if it was one of the worst, forward Ziaire Williams joked. Already the top-ranked offense in the league, the Lakers should strive to match that by becoming a top-10 defense, Redick implored his team. Williams is not stopping there. “Top 10 should be at least like our standard, if not better,” the forward said. “Our half-court defense has been great. Obviously, rebounding has been one of the biggest things for us, cleaning up transition as well. But the potential’s there. We have the size, the length, the athleticism. It’s just about going out there and executing.” Read more: Lakers' Austin Reaves considered day-to-day with heel injury The Lakers, ranked 18th in defensive efficiency, thrive on forcing turnovers and protecting the rim. Their 18.5 turnovers forced per game rank third in the league, and they average an NBA-best 11 steals per game. Center Walker Kessler’s 2.2 blocks per game rank third. But they can’t finish the strong half-court possessions. The Lakers are ranked 28th in defensive rebounding and 25th in second-chance points given up. The Lakers staff rewatched every offensive rebound given up this season. Lack of boxing out was the biggest fault. Then there were instances when players stood and watched. “If I stand and watch and try and outjump someone else, I’m probably not going to get the rebound,” said forward Jake LaRavia, who has been an offensive rebounding revelation since entering the starting lineup, averaging 2.8 offensive rebounds in the last nine games. “So you have to go and be physical and hit bodies, and then just be able to dive on loose balls, finish possessions, it’s really just who’s going to work harder.” Kessler is averaging 8.1 defensive rebounds during the Lakers’ seven-game winning streak — which is the second-longest in Redick’s coaching tenure — compared to 6.3 during the first six games. Forward Jarred Vanderbilt, who did not play in the first four games, has made the most of his limited minutes off the bench, grabbing 7.9 defensive rebounds per 36 minutes, the second-best rate on the team among players who have played more than three minutes. Vanderbilt, averaging 3.8 rebounds per game in 11.9 minutes, had 10 rebounds in less than 14 minutes against the Detroit Pistons on Nov. 8. Transition defense also is sinking the Lakers’ defensive efforts. Opponents are scoring 20.2 points off turnovers per game, which put the Lakers 24th out of 30 teams. Redick blames some of that on the Lakers’ offensive flaws. Although they are the league’s most efficient offense, the Lakers turn the ball over 16.9 times per game, the fifth-most in the NBA. Lakers guard Luka Doncic shoots over two Bucks during a win Wednesday in Milwaukee. (Aaron Gash / Associated Press) Luka Doncic , the league’s leading scorer at 38.6 points per game, also averages an NBA-worst five turnovers. Austin Reaves , who is day-to-day because of a left heel bruise suffered Wednesday against Milwaukee, averages 24.7 points and 3.4 turnovers. Doncic is expected to play Sunday despite tweaking his right ankle late in Wednesday’s win. Reaves didn’t participate in practice Saturday but Collin Sexton was a full participant. The guard wore a thick Band-Aid over his right eyebrow and had bruising around his right eye after bumping heads with Milwaukee’s Ryan Rollins but said he doesn’t expect to wear a mask. He needs only to keep the cut covered to ensure it doesn’t open up again. The rugged guard is familiar with the protocols; Sexton said this was the 11th time in his career that he’s received stitches in his face. The short break offered an important opportunity for players to rest after a grueling three-game Eastern Conference trip. They now enter a softer stretch in the schedule. After Sunday’s game in Phoenix, the Lakers play their next four at home against three teams — Charlotte, Sacramento and Utah, twice — that have a combined six wins. Their next game against a team with a winning record isn’t until Nov. 27 at San Antonio. The 11-2 Spurs, who have won 11 consecutive games, are the only team with an active winning streak longer than the Lakers’. Sign up for our weekly newsletter on all things Lakers. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

stories.title: The Suns are getting crushed in one critical area of the game
stories.summary: The Suns have plenty of early-season problems, but their inability to compete around the basket may be the biggest.
stories.detailText: PHOENIX, AZ - NOVEMBER 12: Moussa Diabate #14 of the Charlotte Hornets boxes out Oso Ighodaro #11 of the Phoenix Suns during the game on November 12, 2026 at Mortgage Matchup Center in Phoenix, Arizona. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Barry Gossage/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images When you look at the Phoenix Suns and see a 5-6 record staring back at you, there are plenty of explanations for why they’ve stumbled out of the gate. One of the most obvious is the schedule. According to ESPN’s strength-of-schedule metrics , Phoenix has faced the third-toughest slate in the NBA through the first 11 games of the season. We can also point to the ongoing challenges surrounding Jalen Green and his inability to consistently find his place on this roster. We can discuss how Miles Bridges has yet to hit his stride as he continues adjusting to a new team, a new system, and new responsibilities. But there’s one glaring deficiency that threatens to haunt the Suns throughout the entire season unless they fundamentally change their approach or somehow miraculously become a larger basketball team overnight. Their inability to impact the game at the rim. And the numbers are downright horrific. Last season, Phoenix finished 29th in the NBA in field goal attempts within five feet of the basket, averaging 23.7 per game. This season? They’re averaging 23.5, the fifth fewest in the league. Think about that for a moment. The Suns have a healthy Jalen Green, a player whose athleticism and explosiveness theoretically provide the ability to get downhill and attack the basket. They also brought in Miles Bridges, another player expected to provide a more physical presence and generate opportunities around the rim. And through 11 games, neither addition has meaningfully moved the needle. Phoenix is attacking the basket at essentially the same rate as last season, despite investing significant resources in players who were supposed to address that very deficiency. But the offensive struggles around the cylinder are only half the problem. The other half? Rebounding. And somehow, the numbers are even uglier. The Suns rank dead last in the NBA in rebounds per game, averaging a miserable 38.9. That’s a full 10 rebounds fewer than the Minnesota Timberwolves, who lead the league at 48.9 per game. Phoenix also ranks 30th in rebounding percentage at 45.2%, meaning opponents are consistently winning the battle for available rebounds. When you begin examining how that translates into actual points, the situation becomes even more alarming. The Suns surrender 18.1 second-chance points per game, the second most in the league. Meanwhile, they’re generating only 12.8 second-chance points themselves, the second fewest. So not only are opponents getting additional opportunities to score, but Phoenix is failing to create those same opportunities on the other end. That’s a pretty brutal combination. If you need a recent example of how dire the situation has become, look no further than Thursday night’s victory over Charlotte. Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Maluach, two of the players Phoenix relies upon to provide some semblance of interior presence, combined for five rebounds. In a game where the Suns were outrebounded by 21. Shall I go on? No matter how you slice it, this is a five-alarm fire for a team attempting to establish itself as a legitimate competitor in the Western Conference. Much like speed, size can’t be taught. You can preach positioning, emphasize boxing out, and demand greater effort on the glass, but there’s only so much coaching can accomplish when your roster consistently finds itself at a physical disadvantage. The most deflating aspect of this deficiency is how it impacts both ends of the floor. Defensively, the Suns can execute an entire possession correctly, rotate effectively, contest shots, and force opponents into difficult attempts. But if they can’t secure the rebound, all that work becomes meaningless. The possession continues, the defense has to scramble again, and another opportunity is handed to the opposition. You cannot consistently give NBA teams extra possessions and expect to win basketball games. It places an enormous burden on your defense, especially when you’re already asking players to compensate for a lack of size and interior physicality. And offensively, the inability to consistently attack and finish around the basket creates an entirely different set of problems. When opposing defenses don’t have to respect your ability to penetrate and score at the rim, they can become more aggressive on the perimeter. They can close out harder, pressure ball handlers, and force you into difficult jump shots because they aren’t particularly concerned about what happens if you get past the initial defender. Perhaps that also helps explain why Phoenix is averaging the second-fewest free throw attempts per game in the NBA. They’re not getting to the rack. It’s an unsustainable combination of deficiencies, particularly for a team that doesn’t possess the overwhelming offensive firepower to compensate for them. The Suns can survive a difficult schedule. They can work through the growing pains associated with integrating new players. They can experiment with rotations, redefine responsibilities, and hope that chemistry improves as the season progresses. But how exactly do you overcome being one of the worst teams in basketball at attacking the rim, rebounding the basketball, and preventing opponents from generating second-chance opportunities? That’s a much more difficult question to answer. And right now, I’m not sure the Phoenix Suns have one. I’m trying to find a little optimism in all of this. The Suns are 5-6, they’ve played one of the toughest schedules in the league, and they have plenty of areas that need improvement. But we’re still early enough in the season for adjustments to matter. Jalen Green can find his footing. Miles Bridges can become more comfortable in his role. The coaching staff can experiment with lineups and find better ways to generate opportunities around the basket. None of that is guaranteed to solve the rebounding problem, and the lack of size remains a legitimate concern. But this team doesn’t need to become a dominant interior force overnight. It needs to become more competitive in the areas that are currently costing it possessions and points. If Phoenix can make even modest progress there, there’s still plenty of season left to build something worthwhile. The problems are real, but so is the opportunity to get better.

stories.title: JJ Redick has lofty defensive identity for Lakers: ‘Physical as f–k’
stories.summary: We all know JJ Redick is a basketball sicko. You know, the type of guy who rewatches games in a dark basement to pore over what he and the Lakers...
stories.detailText: We all know JJ Redick is a basketball sicko. You know, the type of guy who rewatches games in a dark basement to pore over what he and the Lakers could’ve done better. On Friday, we got a glimpse of what his staff is doing behind the scenes. Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick looks on during the first half of an NBA basketball game against the Milwaukee Bucks, Nov. 11, 2026, in Milwaukee. AP Photo/Aaron Gash Redick said his analytics team used the three-day break between games to prepare a 21-page presentation on the Lakers, who have won seven games in a row and have the NBA’s best record at 11-2. The coaches reviewed it for 1 ½ hours on Friday and presented it to the players. “Being first in the West, with the stuff that they showed us, you would think we were almost last, you know?” Ziaire Williams said, flashing a smile. “But gotta keep us honest.” One of the main goals? “We know we want to be a top-10 defense,” Redick said. “We know we are not going to be able to do that unless we become better than a bottom-10 transition team and better than a bottom-10 defensive rebounding team.” While the Lakers are leading the league in steals per game (11), are third in blocks per game (6.2) and are second in total deflections (257), they’re greatly struggling in other areas defensively. The Lakers are rated 18th defensively and 26th in rebounding (40.8). Redick also identified a key area on transition defense he wants to tweak. “Some of the transition stuff is live-ball turnovers,” Redick said. “We’re at a 10% live-ball turnover rate. So one out of every 10 possessions is a live-ball turnover that’s going to create a transition possession.” As for offense? Despite being the top-rated team in the league offensively, the Lakers have multiple areas in which they want to improve, including bolstering their third unit, which has notoriously squandered leads late in games. Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick and Luka Doncic converse with referee James Williams during a game against the Atlanta Hawks on Nov. 9, 2026. Getty Images Redick pointed out that Cameron Carr and Adou Thiero are still playing catch-up after missing time due to various injuries. Lakers assistant coach Scott Brooks is trying to get them up to speed. “He took those guys for a classroom setting [Friday],” Redick said. “We just need to coach them more. Not going to put it all on them. They need to be able to run offense, though. “I think that’s the biggest thing. It’s unacceptable to just consistently be calling offensive plays and then they come down and jack a 3 with 18 on the shot clock. We’re trying to use time and be organized.” Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick reacts on the sidelines during a game against the Atlanta Hawks in Atlanta on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Redick, whom the Lakers hired to take over the helm in June 2024 despite having no prior coaching experience, has shined in his role. He led the Lakers to back-to-back 50-win seasons for the first time since Phil Jackson in 2007-2011. He has a clear idea of what he wants the Lakers’ identity to be on both sides of the court. Offensively? “Organized, unselfish and advantage-based,” he said. Defensively? “Organized, physical as f–k and relentless,” he added.

Injury Report Wizards: Jamir Watkins – Out (Knee), Tristan Vukcevic – Out (Hip), Reece Beekman – Out (Shoulder), Justin Champagnie – Out (Foot), Bub Carrington – Game Time Decision (Chest) Pistons: Steven Adams- Game Time Decision (Calf), Clint Capella – Game Time Decision (Ankle), Marcus Smart – Out (Suspension) Pregame notes Washington has a new addition to its injury report ahead of Sunday night’s matchup against the Rockets. Carrington recorded two points and two assists in 16 minutes before being ruled out for the second overtime period. He now joins Watkins, Vukcevic, Beekman and Champagnie on the injury report, adding another setback for a Wizards team riding a six-game losing streak. Sunday’s matchup with Houston gives Washington another opportunity to earn its first win since Nov. 2, but it won’t come easy. The 10-3 Rockets enter the contest riding a three-game winning streak. Trae Young also delivered a strong performance, leading Washington with 37 points and 15 assists while hitting a clutch three-pointer to send the game to overtime at the end of regulation. Washington also had one of its best nights from beyond the arc this season, knocking down a season-high 14 triples. Carrying that shooting success into Sunday’s matchup will be important if the Wizards hope to keep pace with one of the league’s top teams.

stories.title: Sixers finding success manufacturing their own energy
stories.summary: The Sixers on Thursday did what great teams do, overcoming a sleepy start to take care of business.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA, PA - NOVEMBER 12: Anfernee Simons #5 of the Philadelphia 76ers drives to the basket during the game against the Toronto Raptors on November 12, 2026 at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Nathaniel S. Butler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images It was only the first quarter of the 13th game of the Sixers’ season, so there seemed to be no cause for alarm (and never mind the booing). Still, they were down 17 to a Toronto team on the second half of a back-to-back and playing without its two best players. There was at least the possibility Thursday that it was one of those nights every NBA team has on occasion, where the mood and the energy and the desire are just … off. It would be easy to reach that conclusion, after Boston smacked the Sixers around Tuesday, in what was supposed to be the Jaylen Brown Revenge Game. Also, LeBron James sat out against the Raptors. The official reason was “low back/sciatica management,” though this seems comparable to that time years ago when the Spurs rested Tim Duncan and listed him this way in the boxscore: “DNP-OLD.” When Nick Nurse called timeout with 2:40 left in the first and his team down 32-16, he said he was thinking in the simplest terms. “I just want the players to play well,” he said, adding that everyone seemed to be searching for a rhythm, or seeking to “shake something off from the last game or whatever,” as he put it. They fell 17 back moments later, but soon found their inspiration, soon manufactured their own energy. Reserves Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker found it by looking back to their time on some wretched Portland teams. VJ Edgecombe found it by looking forward to a potential spot in the NBA slam-dunk contest. And Tyrese Maxey found it by looking over to the sideline, to his infant daughter. The end result was a 123-112 Sixers victory over the Scottie Barnes – and Kawhi Leonard -less Raptors. Maxey scored 27, and Joel Embiid , who limped off in the first quarter after bumping knees with a Raptor, returned and finished with 20. Edgecombe enjoyed a Swiss Army Knife kinda night – 15 points, eight rebounds, eight assists, three steals and a block – and the bench brigade of Simons, Walker and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope contributed 37 points, including 9-for-12 three-point sniping. “You learn once you’re coming off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there,” Simons said after going 5-for-6 from the arc and scoring 17. What he read before checking in at the aforementioned timeout was straight out of the Stephen King collection. So the idea, Simons said, was to “bring some energy and some life to the team.” He provided the night’s first thunderbolt, nailing a three-ball at the first-period buzzer to cut the deficit to nine. “Those are big momentum plays,” Nurse said, “that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment.” From that point forward, the Sixers, now 10-3, seemed inevitable. Edgecombe turned a second-quarter steal into a breakaway slam. Maxey threw an alley-oop to Brown from midcourt for a bucket late in the third, when Philadelphia went ahead for good. And with the Raptors hanging around late in the fourth, Simons and Caldwell-Pope (11 points) connected from three to put it away. Re Simons: Now in his ninth NBA season, he is playing for his fourth team. He has been productive everywhere he’s been, but this year his minutes (21.7) and points (10.2) are down from their usual levels. He says he doesn’t care – not after playing on losing teams five of the seven seasons he spent in Portland, his first stop. The Blazers were 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46 the last three of those seasons, when Walker was a teammate. (Another Sixer, Rayan Rupert , was on two of those teams.) “You learn a lot in those situations about yourself, the people around you, your teammates,” Simons said, adding that “you feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you’re winning. And so that’s something that you can’t take for granted for sure, because it’s hard to win in the NBA.” Sometimes it’s hard to even get on the court, as Walker has learned. He is averaging 15 minutes a game over five seasons, but now looms as the best option to back up Embiid at center, despite standing 6-7. Not to worry, he said after contributing nine points and eight boards in just under 16 minutes Thursday; his dad, Samaki , had been a small-ball center himself while playing a decade in the Association. The younger Walker knows the assignment, knows what the job entails. He’s also healthy this season, having undergone offseason knee surgery. And while it wasn’t clear where he might fit in the pecking order after the Sixers revamped their roster over the summer, he had high hopes. “I don’t know if I was delusional,” he said, “but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part. I read some things, and they say it’s a surprise. But if you were around me this summer and saw the mindset I had, then it wouldn’t be a surprise. So this is expected, and I just want to continue to get better.” There were also questions about Edgecombe’s role coming into the season. But his attitude is always exemplary, his approach relentless. Informed after Thursday’s game that the only guard in the league with more dunks than him was Houston’s Amen Thompson , he scoffed. “Man, he don’t even count,” Edgecombe said. He might have a point. Thompson stands 6-7. Edgecombe is listed at 6-4, but attacks the rim so regularly that he is musing about the dunk contest on All-Star Weekend, February in Phoenix. “Obviously I don’t want to sit here and give a yes, and I don’t want to give a no,” he said. “But that’s something I’m thinking about, for sure.” Maxey couldn’t help but think about his daughter Marvel. Born May 14 to Tyrese and his girlfriend Myra Gordon, she attended her first game with her mom Thursday – “a really cool moment,” as Maxey said. She might not be back for a while, though. “It’s too late,” he said. “She was yawning and doing a whole bunch of stuff.” So too were the Sixers for a while. They awakened from their slumber. They found their footing, manufactured their own energy. On many, many nights across the long season, that’s how it has to be.

stories.title: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo showcase Heat's potential in win vs. Cavs
stories.summary: Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo each scored 37 points to help the Heat top the Cavaliers for their sixth win in eight games.
stories.detailText: MIAMI -- Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo had their best performances of the season as a duo Friday night to help the Heat show their lofty potential as an East contender in a 133-121 win over the Cavaliers . Adebayo had 37 points and 14 rebounds, prompting Antetokounmpo to praise him as "one of the most versatile bigs I've ever played with." Antetokounmpo added 37 points and nine rebounds. The Heat improved to 2-0 in the NBA Cup and moved back to .500 (6-6) after winning six of their past eight games. "Bam played great, aggressive, got to his spots. I did the same," Antetokounmpo said. "Every game will look differently. There will be times like tonight where we will overpower other bigs, but we can't force it." It was a statement win for the Heat, whose two stars showed growth while they try to master their unique fit on the court. Against the Cavaliers, they looked like the best frontcourt in the NBA, as many predicted in the offseason. "We're making progress in trust. We need to keep doing our work quietly, humbly," Antetokounmpo said. "There's still a lot of work to be done. We're not even close. Still a lot of work to be done." The catalyst for Miami's standout performance Friday night was Adebayo, who was aggressive as a scorer, rebounder and defender. During a four-minute stretch early in the fourth quarter, he took over in all phases with Antetokounmpo on the bench. Asked about his dominant four-minute stretch, Adebayo said, "That's my unit." He added that he "had to get in my rhythm" when asked about his big night. Heat coach Erik Spoelstra pointed out Adebayo's play early in the fourth quarter, noting that Adebayo's superpower is "how he can connect a group to embrace a challenge and use his force of will." The Heat are starting to play with confidence and having fun again after an 0-4 start, which forced the group to focus on communication and building chemistry. The rewards are starting to surface. Spoelstra said he began to see a difference three weeks ago and was confident the Heat would explode offensively. "Bam and Giannis, they are supposed to carry us with their force. Will the stat line always look like that? I don't know," Spoelstra said. "That's a lot of force that they're putting on the opponent in the paint. They're both playing with confidence and when they get to their spots, but it was a force and physicality that the opponent has to feel when those two guys are on the floor. That's our advantage." Both stars gave a shoutout to point guard Davion Mitchell , who had 22 points and a career-high 17 assists. "That's insane," Antetokounmpo said. The Heat host the Detroit Pistons on the second leg of a back-to-back set Saturday. Guard Klay Thompson said he hopes to play after missing Friday's game because of left ankle soreness.

stories.title: Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security
stories.summary: Sacramento Kings head Doug Christie has seen a lot of losses but here's what he said about being on a hot seat with the organization.
stories.detailText: SACRAMENTO ― The Sacramento Kings have dropped another game and if you think head coach Doug Christie is worried about being in some kind of hot seat, he's not. And he shouldn't be. It's a familiar position for Christie, who's been dealt a bad hand since his head coaching tenure began. He inherited a then-Mike Brown team that was a season removed from the postseason before eventually trading its franchise player, De'Aaron Fox. They finished 40-42, Christie went 27-24 as interim, having taken over after a 13-18 start. Last season, as an official first-year coach, without the interim tag, multiple players in his projected lineup, including Domantas Sabonis and Keegan Murray, missed large portions of the season, and the Kings finished with its worst record in franchise history since moving to Sacramento at 22-60. And now, the Kings are having one of the worst starts in franchise history, dropping to 1-11 after their Friday night loss to the Portland Trail Blazers, 120-107, on Nov. 13 during the NBA Cup. It's the worst start since the 1990-91 season, in which that team started 1-13. "I think this seat is hot always, so it doesn't really matter," Christie told USA TODAY about potentially being in the hot seat. "Obviously, we want to win games. Nobody wants to win more than me, from the standpoint that the record doesn't go on the player's numbers. The record goes on coach's number." When Scott Perry became Kings general manager in April 2025, one of his first moves was to sign Christie to a three-year deal, worth about $2 million per year with a team option in the final year, 2027-28. Christie remained leading the charge after coaching to the worst franchise record in team history since 2008-2009 (17-65), as Perry attributed that tumultuous season to injuries , according to The Athletic. It's much of the same this season, with a season-ending injury to Ben Simmons and second-year center Maxime Raynaud missing the start of the season with a knee injury. "We come in, continue to teach, continue to push," Christie said. "As we get all these guys back and get them healthy, and then we continue down the path of trying to put together what we thought we would be putting together when we started this process." It's not Doug Christie's fault, Mike Bibby says The Kings are reportedly hesitant to part ways with Christie, according to The Athletic's Sam Amick. Former Sacramento Kings legend and current Sacramento State head coach Mike Bibby sat front row to get a witness of the the beatdown handed to the Kings. The former guard, who played in Sacramento from 2001-2008, showed support for his former teammate, saying he wasn't the one to blame during a postgame appearance with Morgan Ragan and Deuce Mason on NBC Sports California. "I don't blame Doug (Christie)," Bibby said. "I don't think Doug is the problem. Doug's been there for a long time, I think Doug could help, but getting rid of Doug's not the problem." However, Bibby did say it was "time for some changes". Although he wasn't sure where those changes needed to come from, he advised the team to trade guys like Domantas Sabonis, Zach LaVine and Malik Monk to put them in better positions while the Kings start over. It happened to Bibby in his day when the Kings were no longer winning and they traded him to the Atlanta Hawks in 2008. "When I was here I didn't wanna leave, but it was time to go," Bibby said. "For those guys put them in good situations like Sabonis, LaVine, put them in situations that could help them and get some good stuff back. It's going to take a couple of years to get the Kings going again." Kings: Darius Acuff Jr. is making history, but is losing taking a toll? Kings' message to the fans If there's one thing Christie knows, it's how hard the Sacramento fans go for the Kings. He's experienced it as a player, and as both assistant and head coach he's seen how they've stuck beside the team through multiple years of losing seasons and the breakthrough when they finally cracked the postseason after a 16-year drought. Christie's message to the fans: "it won't always be like this." "This is a process that we're going through to try to get to where we want to go, and their loyalty means everything," Christie told USA TODAY. " When I see them around town, they're always (saying) 'coach keep going, keep pushing,' and that's what I do every day. I'll always be the first one in the building, working until we figure this thing out." Kings forward Keegan Murray had a similar message to the fans to keep supporting, despite the shortcomings. "I love our fans. They've been great to us... to me. I appreciate them coming out to support, we know that Rome's not built in a day but at the end of the day we're trying," Murray told USA TODAY. "With their support, it'll only get better." Murray, Sabonis and Monk are the few Kings players that have been around for their lone playoff appearance in the last 15 years. Murray often tells the team, especially Acuff who was down in the dumps after a recent home loss , about how loud Golden 1 Center can get when their team is rolling. "When we're really good, this place is better than any arena in the NBA," Murray said. "I feel like that's a big motivating factor in what we're trying to get to. ... I'm just hoping we can get back on track." .oembed-frame {width:100%;height:100%;margin:0;border:0;} This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security

stories.title: Sixers, Brown have a ‘humbling' night in loss to Celtics
stories.summary: Jaylen Brown called the Sixers' blowout defeat to the Celtics “humbling.”
stories.detailText: Sixers, Brown have a ‘humbling' night in loss to Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia Whatever Jaylen Brown and the Sixers dreamed up for their first matchup against the Celtics soon flew out the window on Tuesday night. Brown was whistled for two early fouls, the Sixers fell behind and their early-season flaws were on full display in a 123-101 loss at Xfinity Mobile Arena. “We’ve just got to get better,” Brown said. “Tonight was humbling. We got outplayed, out-executed. So we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the next one.” Over 26 minutes, Brown had 13 points on 4-for-9 shooting and five rebounds against the team that traded him away this summer. As for the endless dissection of his relationship with former co-star Jayson Tatum , Brown didn’t have much to add Tuesday. There was no public reconciliation, no obvious on-court animosity and generally nothing to satisfy fans hoping for some kind of fireworks on that front. The pregame moment between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown. 📺 NBA on NBC and Peacock pic.twitter.com/P4iclUnqZ5 — NBA on NBC and Peacock (@NBAonNBC) November 11, 2026 “I’m just focused on doing what’s best for my team,” Brown said. “Everything else … to be honest, I wasn’t paying attention. But credit to Jayson; he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics. They executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and they were the better team tonight.” Tatum scored 21 points, two of which came on a third-quarter slam over LeBron James. Paul George continued his fantastic start as a Celtic by dropping 36 points and draining six three-pointers. The Celtics dominated from beyond the arc, shooting 22 for 49 (44.9 percent). The Sixers went just 11 for 37 (29.7 percent) on another night of underwhelming offense. The team sits 22nd in the NBA in offensive rating , 24th in three-point makes per game and 21st in three-point percentage. “I think that we’ve got some guys that are obviously shooting much lower percentages than their last season or their career average — almost a handful of guys,” Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. “And I don’t think it’s because they’re shooting fallaway, totally contested ones. I think they’re shots we want them to take. So I think they’ll continue to take ‘em and I’m pretty sure those will even out into their career averages.” Joel Embiid is at 37 percent from the floor and 4 for 33 from three-point range (12.1 percent). The Sixers’ seven-time All-Star center got through an injury scare when he rolled his ankle late in the second quarter and hit a three early in the third. It was his first long-range make since the Sixers’ home opener back on Oct. 22. “It’s a work in progress,” Embiid said. “I think the biggest thing is just not thinking. I’m probably overthinking it. The rhythm of the game is different. I’m so used to having to create for myself, so it’s a little bit different. “But I think I’m slowly getting better. You could see as soon as I made a three, the next shot in the short corner … I didn’t even think about it. I just shot it and let it fly, and I made it. … I think it’s just about taking what’s in front of you. Make or miss, keep working on your game. It’s going to get there at some point.” Even with the Sixers second in the Eastern Conference standings at 9-3, Embiid believes the team’s defense has “slacked off a little bit” in recent games. “I don’t really look at the record,” he said. “I just look at the process of, ‘Are we getting better every day?’ We can always do a better job at all phases of the game.” Boston’s now first in the East at 9-2. “They’re one of the top teams in the league and they’ve been together for a while,” Brown said. “We’ve got a lot to work on over here, so we’ve got to get to work.” The Sixers will face the Raptors on Thursday night in Philadelphia. They’ll have to wait until Jan. 21 in Boston to see the Celtics again. “I was looking forward to this,” Brown said. “I was looking forward to playing well, but s— happens. Just get ready for the next one.”

stories.title: ‘Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles
stories.summary: Former Blazers teammates are contributing in different ways for a Sixers team built to contend.
stories.detailText: ‘Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker shared the floor for 128 games in Portland. The Trail Blazers won 43 of them. They sat beside one another in the Sixers’ interview room Thursday night after a victory and discussed what the other 85 taught them. “Whether you’ve got a big role or a small role, it’s hard to win in the NBA,” Simons said. “We’ve seen it firsthand.” Their roles were considerably different then. Simons was an established starter entrusted with creating and scoring. Walker, a 2022 second-round pick, was trying to establish himself in a rotation. During their three overlapping seasons, Portland went 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46. The Blazers missed the playoffs each year. Both are now reserves on a Sixers team constructed to contend. In nine games they’ve both appeared in this season, Philadelphia is 7-2. They provided 26 points, 11 rebounds and six three-pointers in the Sixers’ 123-112 win over the Raptors at Xfinity Mobile Arena. Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range. Walker recorded nine points and eight rebounds, including four on the offensive glass. The Sixers outscored Toronto by 24 points during Simons’ 23 minutes. Neither former Blazer committed a turnover. Their production helped Philadelphia overcome a 17-point first-quarter deficit and improve to 10-3 without LeBron James. “You learn once you come off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there,” Simons said. “Obviously, we started off kind of slow. You just want to go in, bring some energy, get some stops, get out and run. I think everybody who got off the bench brought energy.” Simons supplied an immediate lift with a deep three-pointer at the first-quarter buzzer. His shot ended an 8-0 Sixers run and trimmed Toronto’s lead to nine. He remained involved during an 11-0 burst late in the third quarter, knocking down a three and setting up Walker for a basket. Walker then made a three early in the fourth before Simons scored on the Sixers’ next possession. When Toronto pulled within six with less than five minutes remaining, Simons answered with his fifth three-pointer. Making those shots is the most obvious way Simons can help a roster already featuring James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown. He said the Sixers have not made him feel as though every opportunity must go in. “They encourage us to keep shooting the ball,” Simons said. “Knowing that a team has that much confidence in us to keep shooting makes the game that much easier. Whether you miss or make, as long as we get the right shots in the right moments, I think everybody can live with the misses and makes.” Simons spent seven seasons in Portland before playing last year with Boston and Chicago. His move to Philadelphia reunited him with Walker and Rayan Rupert, another former Blazer who joined the Sixers on a two-way contract during the offseason. Knowing familiar faces awaited him helped Simons enter another new locker room. “It made the transition seamless,” he said. “Just being able to have some comfortability with guys that I played with for multiple years. It’s been fun, kind of feeling like a little bit of old times. Me, Bari and Rups have been through a lot.” Walker’s path to Philadelphia began a year earlier and required an additional step. After playing 188 games over three seasons with Portland, Walker signed a two-way contract with the Sixers in July 2025. He earned a standard contract in February and has since pushed his way into the backup-center conversation despite standing 6-foot-7. Walker believes some of the work he did on losing teams was easily missed. “When I first got to the league, I was part of a rebuilding process,” he said. “I just felt like some of the little things I did didn’t always get noticed when you’re losing. I told myself, if I ever got to be part of a winning organization, then I’d go out and expand my abilities.” Rebounding has made Walker difficult for Nick Nurse to overlook. Walker credited his timing and strong hands to lessons passed down by his father, former NBA center Samaki Walker. Those instincts have become especially useful while the Sixers piece together their frontcourt behind Embiid. “Rebounding is a skill I kind of honed in on,” Walker said. “My dad was a good rebounder. He was known for his rebounding and his timing. I think it’s just a gift that he transferred to me.” Walker has made it clear that he expected to earn a role this season. “I don’t know if I was delusional, but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part,” he said. “I read something where they said it’s a surprise, but if you were around me this summer, it wouldn’t be a surprise. This is expected, and I just want to continue to get better.” The freedom Simons once had in Portland is no longer necessary. Walker does not need a high volume of touches, either. Both understand that playing beside the Sixers’ stars requires shooting when open, moving the ball and handling the less glamorous work. “You’ve got to find ways to impact the game multiple ways, even if you’re not scoring,” Simons said. “Whether it’s cutting, making the right read and pass to Joel, being the right swing pass to VJ, boxing out on defense or just being in the right position.” Their opportunities will fluctuate. Simons may take nine shots one night and only a few the next. Walker’s minutes will depend on matchups and the health of Philadelphia’s frontcourt. Winning has changed what they are being asked to do. Their three years together in Portland taught them why the adjustment is worthwhile. “You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you’re winning,” Simons said. “That’s something you can’t take for granted.”

stories.title: Embiid and James listed as questionable for Sixers vs. Raptors
stories.summary: The Sixers listed both Joel Embiid and LeBron James as questionable for their game against the Raptors.
stories.detailText: Embiid and James listed as questionable for Sixers vs. Raptors originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia The Sixers listed both Joel Embiid and LeBron James as questionable for their Thursday night game vs. the Raptors. As has been the case on previous early-season injury reports, James’ official listing was “low back/sciatica management” and Embiid’s was “right foot plantar fascia injury management.” While Thursday’s contest isn’t part of a back-to-back, it’s the sort of situation in which the Sixers have load management matters in mind for the 32-year-old Embiid and 41-year-old James. They’ll host the Pacers on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET and then visit the Nets the following night. James logged 29 minutes Tuesday in the 9-3 Sixers’ loss to the Celtics and Embiid went 31. Embiid said postgame that he rolled his ankle late in the second quarter, but he was fine to play the second half. With the Raptors facing Boston on Wednesday night, Toronto’s complete injury report won’t be available until Thursday afternoon. The Raptors announced Tuesday that superstar Kawhi Leonard will be sidelined for at least one more week because of his left knee injury. Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear) will all remain out for the Sixers against the Raptors.

stories.title: Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win
stories.summary: The Sixers brushed off their blowout loss to the Celtics and got back in the win column Thursday night.
stories.detailText: Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia The Sixers brushed off their blowout loss to the Celtics and got back in the win column Thursday night. They overcame a first-quarter deficit as high as 17 points and earned a 123-112 home win over the Raptors. The Sixers moved to 10-3 and Toronto fell to 5-7. Tyrese Maxey had 27 points and eight assists. Joel Embiid added 20 points. Jaylen Brown tallied 18 points and six rebounds. VJ Edgecombe posted 15 points, eight rebounds and a season-high eight assists. Anfernee Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range. RJ Barrett recorded 31 points and 14 rebounds. Immanuel Quickley had 26 points and six assists. The Sixers were without LeBron James (low back/sciatica management), Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear). The team told reporters Thursday morning that Bona will be re-evaluated in approximately one week and that Barlow participated in shootaround. The 23-year-old forward also went through a pregame workout on the Xfinity Mobile Arena floor. There’s no formal timetable for his return. Toronto’s sidelined players included Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes. The Sixers will face the Pacers on Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. Here are observations on their victory over the Raptors: Embiid exits early but returns to action Dean Wade began the game in James’ normal spot. The Sixers started slowly, missing their first foul field goals and opening 1 for 8 from three-point range. Embiid had an early injury scare. He stayed down after setting a ball screen and having an apparent knee-to-knee collision with Ja’Kobe Walter. The Sixers called timeout with 8:30 left in the first quarter and Embiid grabbed at his right knee. He eventually rose with assistance from teammates and Sixers head athletic trainer Kevin Johnson, then limped back to the locker room. Jabari Walker entered. At the 5:26 mark of the first quarter, Embiid checked back in to cheers from the home fans. “I knew that he didn’t twist it or anything,” Maxey said. “I knew it was a knee-to-knee, so I wasn’t too worried. He kept saying, ‘I just got kneed.’ That still hurts, though.” Embiid ended up logging 28 minutes, though he certainly wanted to play more. “He was very, very motivated to play,” Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. “It was hard to get him out for his scheduled rests tonight, which is a good problem sometimes.” While Embiid’s return was a major positive development, the Sixers fell further behind. The Raptors’ lead swelled to 32-16 with a Jamison Battle three-pointer and Nurse burned a timeout. Brown-Edgecombe pair strong in 2nd quarter Simons sunk a buzzer-beating three to conclude the first quarter, cutting the Sixers’ deficit to nine points. “Those are big momentum plays that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment,” Nurse said. The Sixers kept rolling against a shorthanded Toronto team playing on the second night of a back-to-back. Simons nailed a triple to kick off the scoring in the second quarter. Brown buried a mid-range jumper and Edgecombe jammed in a crowd-pleasing dunk to give the Sixers a 35-34 edge. Brown and Edgecombe shined in the second quarter both as individuals and as a duo. The Sixers need Edgecombe to attack a bit more offensively when he shares the floor with Brown and bench players. It doesn’t hurt for the second-year guard to have that clarity about his role in those units. “He’s one of our better playmakers,” Maxey said of Edgecombe. “He’s really good at getting downhill and creating for himself and others.” The Sixers’ only three bench rotation players were Walker, Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope (11 points, five assists). In addition to Walker, Wade got center minutes behind Embiid. Maxey, Sixers pull away Embiid picked up his third foul with 2:23 left in the second quarter and had to take a seat. The teams were tied at 60 apiece through two periods. The game remained even for much of the third, but Maxey fueled an 11-0 Sixers run late in the quarter. His speed and the Sixers’ collective focus on pushing the pace whenever possible allowed the team to get regular points before Toronto could set its defense. Maxey zoomed in for a layup, then tossed the ball ahead to Brown for an easy bucket. Brown assisted a Simons three. Walker converted a fast-break lay-in and canned a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter. All of a sudden, the Sixers held a 101-87 lead. Brown, Edgecombe and the bench gave the Sixers more good minutes early in the fourth quarter. They sealed the deal without any late drama. And the fans chanting for a Tacko Fall appearance got their wish with a final-minute entrance by the 7-foot-6 center.

stories.title: Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36
stories.summary: Round 1 of the new-look Sixers vs. the new-look Celtics decisively went Boston’s way on Tuesday night.
stories.detailText: Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia Round 1 of the new-look Sixers vs. the new-look Celtics decisively went Boston’s way on Tuesday night. In the first meeting between the teams since the July trade that sent Jaylen Brown to Philadelphia and Paul George to Boston , the Celtics earned a 123-101 win at Xfinity Mobile Arena. The Sixers dropped to 9-3 and the Celtics improved to 9-2. George was the game’s brightest star, scoring 36 points on 14-for-22 shooting. Jayson Tatum added 21 points. Tyrese Maxey’s 24 points led the Sixers. Brown was hampered by foul trouble in his heavily anticipated first outing against Tatum . He posted 13 points, five rebounds and two assists in 26 minutes. The Sixers will host the Raptors on Thursday night. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Celtics: Brown vs. Tatum takes center stage To no one’s surprise, Brown and Tatum guarded each other to open the night. VJ Edgecombe defended a former teammate in George , who scored Boston’s first four points with a pair of pure jumpers. On the other end, Maxey made the Sixers’ first three field goals. Judging by volume, the home fans cared most about the much-scrutinized Brown vs. Tatum matchup. The crowd was excited early when Brown snagged a steal and then dished to Maxey for a fast-break three-pointer. The fans also dialed up the noise when Brown sized up Tatum in isolation. He wound up dribbling the ball off his foot and out of bounds. Tatum pointed to signal it was Celtics ball. Boston’s star forward had a productive first quarter, posting 11 points. He scored an easy two when he used a back screen to break free from Brown and convert a layup that put the Celtics up 11-7. Boston began 9 for 12 from the floor as a team. As for Brown, he sat shortly after being called for his second foul with 6:48 left in the first quarter. Rough going for Sixers from long distance Brown re-entered at the start of the second quarter. The Sixers still struggled to eat into Boston’s lead. A Sam Hauser triple extended the Celtics’ advantage to 12 points. There was some audible frustration in the building after Brown missed two free throws on the next possesion. The Sixers’ deficit hit 16 points on a Hugo Gonzalez jumper. Meanwhile, the Sixers missed 12 of their first 14 three-point tries. While some of those shots were open looks that simply didn’t go down, the Sixers also rushed up several contested jumpers before they made Boston’s defense do serious work. In the bigger picture, it wouldn’t be remotely surprising if shooting stands out as a weak area for the Sixers come the trade deadline. They entered the game ranked 27th in the NBA in three-point frequency outside of garbage time and 22nd in three-point accuracy, according to Cleaning the Glass. George and Tatum lead the way Joel Embiid (16 points, six rebounds) had an injury scare late in the second quarter when he fell hard after missing a layup in transition. He rose gingerly and limped through the final 30 seconds or so of the first half. The Sixers’ star big man was fine to start the third quarter and even drained a long-overdue three on the opening possession. He’d been in a terrible outside shooting slump (3 for 32 from deep on the season) before that shot. Brown’s foul trouble persisted. He picked up his fourth personal with 10:40 to go in the third quarter. The Sixers stormed back without him and their defense played a large role. After LeBron James rumbled in for a layup, Dean Wade stonewalled Payton Pritchard on the perimeter to force a shot-clock violation. Wade later canned a three to even the contest at 76-all. The Celtics responded and Tatum led the charge. His third-quarter exploits included a highlight slam on James and a top-of-the-key three to build Boston’s lead back up to nine points. Pritchard buried a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter and the Celtics’ advantage kept growing. George celebrated a triple that stretched his team’s lead to 100-82. The Sixers’ spirits were considerably lower as they headed to their bench for a timeout. As a Sixer, George only had one higher-scoring game (39 points) than his performance Tuesday. George and Tatum were each excellent in Philadelphia. Outside of Maxey, who finished 8 for 12 from the field, the Sixers didn’t receive similar games from their stars. Brown will be back in Boston on Jan. 21 when the Sixers visit the Celtics. He’ll try to even the score.

stories.title: Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors
stories.summary: Toronto’s pressure defense, work on the glass and unusual three-point night present Philadelphia with several immediate challenges.
stories.detailText: Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia The Sixers will not need to wait long for an opportunity to move past their most lopsided loss of the season. Less than 48 hours after Boston’s 123-101 win exposed several of Philadelphia’s early weaknesses, the Sixers will host the Toronto Raptors on Thursday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena. The Raptors are coming off a difficult meeting with the Celtics, too. Toronto led Boston by 22 points Wednesday before being outscored 61-34 over the final 29:24 of a 98-93 loss. Philadelphia enters at 9-3 following Tuesday’s defeat . Toronto is 5-6 and will complete a back-to-back and its third game in four nights. LeBron James has been ruled out because of low-back and sciatica management. Joel Embiid is questionable with right plantar fascia injury management. Toronto will be without Kawhi Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Nate Bittle. Here are four areas to watch as the Sixers try to respond. The possession battle Few teams have forced opponents into mistakes as frequently as Toronto. The Raptors have generated 18.9 turnovers per game, the highest mark in the NBA. They are also averaging 10.9 steals and nearly 15 offensive rebounds. The Sixers have countered that type of pressure well. Their 13.0 turnovers per game are tied for one of the lowest marks in the league. Something will have to give. Toronto’s length remains disruptive even without Leonard and Barnes. The Raptors regularly crowd ball handlers, reach into passing lanes and send multiple players toward the offensive glass. Jakob Poeltl supplies size inside while RJ Barrett, Ja’Kobe Walter and Collin Murray-Boyles can create problems away from the ball. The Raptors’ pressure can punish a careless pass twice. It takes away a Sixers possession and gives Toronto an opportunity to score before the defense gets organized. Philadelphia has largely avoided those mistakes while adjusting to a new lineup and playing at a quicker pace. Maintaining that control without James, who has handled a significant share of the playmaking, will be one of Thursday’s clearest challenges. Keeping Toronto out of the open floor Toronto has not built its offense around half-court shooting. The Raptors are averaging 49.6 paint points and 16.4 fast-break points. Even while shorthanded Wednesday, they scored 18 points in transition against Boston. That presents a direct test for a Sixers defense allowing 16.5 fast-break points per game, the fourth-highest figure in the NBA. Philadelphia has also surrendered 49.5 paint points per contest. The first concern will be slowing the ball. Immanuel Quickley returned Wednesday after missing two games with right hamstring soreness. He gives Toronto another guard capable of attacking early in the shot clock, while Barrett has consistently looked to get downhill with Leonard and Barnes unavailable. Poeltl can create scoring chances without having a play called for him. He runs the floor, screens for Toronto’s guards, rolls toward the rim and cleans up misses. The Sixers have been effective in transition themselves, averaging 17.1 fast-break points. Maxey and VJ Edgecombe can change ends quickly after a stop, but Philadelphia must secure the ball first. Thursday’s game could swing on which team gets to run and which one is forced to create against a set defense. Another unpredictable night from three? Toronto provided an extreme example Wednesday of how quickly the three-point line can alter a game. The Raptors entered their matchup against Boston shooting 31.8 percent from beyond the arc. They proceeded to hit 10 of their 18 attempts in the first quarter, tying a franchise record for threes in a period. They went 6 for 25 over the final three quarters. After Wednesday, Toronto is shooting 32.4 percent from three this season. The Sixers should not treat the Raptors like an elite perimeter team. They also cannot allow them to find early confidence through uncovered catch-and-shoot attempts. Walter made five threes Wednesday and scored a team-high 17 points. Rookie Allen Graves added 13 points, while Quickley, Barrett and Jamison Battle are all willing shooters when the ball reaches them in rhythm. Philadelphia’s problems against Boston extended beyond the Celtics making difficult shots. The Sixers were late on several closeouts and occasionally allowed too much separation while navigating screens. Toronto does not rely on the three as heavily as Boston. Wednesday showed it can still build a lead quickly when those shots start falling. Using the schedule advantage The Raptors expended significant energy Wednesday before traveling to Philadelphia. They scored 38 first-quarter points, built a 22-point lead and then watched Boston erase the entire margin before the end of the third quarter. Quickley and Barrett each played more than 31 minutes. Poeltl and Walter both played at least 29. The Sixers should have the fresher legs. Whether they take advantage could become apparent early. Philadelphia has averaged 26.3 first-quarter points with a minus-2.2 scoring margin in opening periods. Slow starts have forced the Sixers to play from behind several times, including in their 29-point comeback against Cleveland. An aggressive start would make Toronto respond quickly after a draining loss. Maxey and Edgecombe can apply pressure by pushing the ball after defensive rebounds instead of allowing the Raptors to set their pressure defense. James’ absence will require an adjustment. Maxey, Brown and Anfernee Simons should handle more of the ball and more of the decisions that come with initiating the offense. If Embiid plays, the Sixers can make Toronto work through Poeltl by establishing him inside. If Embiid sits, Philadelphia’s size concerns will become more pronounced with Adem Bona, Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti also unavailable. The Sixers have a rest advantage against a depleted opponent coming off an emotional loss. Their response should begin well before the fourth quarter.

stories.title: Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return
stories.summary: PG-13, the former Sixer, poured in 36 points, then explained the baseline exchange that gave his return an R rating.
stories.detailText: Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia PG-13 was rated R in his return to Philadelphia. The middle finger Paul George directed toward one baseline fan only reinforced that rating. Tuesday night was expected to revolve around Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum sharing an NBA court as opponents for the first time. Instead, the other headliner in the summer’s blockbuster trade stole the show. George scored a game-high 36 points in Boston’s 123-101 win over the Sixers. He shot 14 for 22 from the floor, made six of his 11 three-point attempts and scored 14 consecutive Boston points in the fourth quarter. The game was tied at 79 with 3:19 remaining in the third quarter. Boston outscored Philadelphia 44-22 from that point forward. The Celtics went nine minutes and 20 seconds without making a two-point field goal during the second half. Instead, they made nine consecutive field goals from three, the second-longest such streak by a Sixers opponent over the last 30 seasons. Payton Pritchard opened the fourth with consecutive threes. George followed with eight straight points, helping the Celtics begin the quarter on a 14-0 run that turned a competitive game into a rout. George’s return carried a complicated history. His two seasons with the Sixers were repeatedly interrupted by injuries, but he also played a significant role in their most memorable playoff run in years. Last spring, George helped the Sixers overcome a 3-1 deficit to eliminate Boston in seven games. He averaged 17.4 points and shot 55 percent from three during the series. Tyrese Maxey was happy to see his former teammate Tuesday, even if he disliked what followed. “It was good to see Paul,” Maxey said. “I love him, love his family. … He gave us everything he had while he was here. We know what he did in the playoffs last year. Great person, great family, and we’ll see him again.” Maxey then added one important qualifier. “I wanted him to score zero points.” George instead scored from nearly everywhere. “He had some open threes. He had some pull-up threes. He had some middies,” Maxey said. “He played within the game, too. That’s what Paul does. He plays within the game. He takes what the defense gives him, and we gave him too many open looks tonight. “PG, we know what PG does. We shouldn’t even be allowing him to get up 11 threes, and that’s on us.” Nick Nurse watched George attack the Sixers in several ways. “He really had it going,” Nurse said. “He’d post up, and-one, fallaways. He went down the lane, high archer off the glass, and-one. He scored in about every way he could tonight.” George heard boos during his return and said the arena carried the atmosphere, though not quite the intensity, of a playoff game. “This building can be very electric as well,” George said. “It was fun. It was fun to play in this environment.” One interaction extended beyond the usual reception for a returning player. During a stoppage, the ball rolled toward a fan seated along the baseline. George said the fan looked directly at him before dropping the ball instead of returning it. “There was a fan being an a–,” George said. “The ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes, dropped the ball on the ground as if I’m a dog to go fetch or go get it, instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do. “And so, yeah, then I rolled him a middle finger in return.”

stories.title: Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double
stories.summary: The Sixers improved to 3-0 Saturday night by beating the Bucks at Xfinity Mobile Arena.
stories.detailText: Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season. Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists. On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards. The Sixers’ absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team’s matchup with the Pistons on Sunday. Here are observations on the Sixers’ victory Saturday: Wade debuts, Embiid starts in style Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James’ place. He’d missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain. The 3-and-D forward scored the night’s first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession. Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team’s offense in the early going. The Sixers’ seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man. Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead. One of Embiid’s assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter. Second-quarter struggles The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn’t enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter. Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run. Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn’t carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly. Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins’ three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead. The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they’d fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win. The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team’s transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game’s first 19 fast-break points. Star trio produces The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup. Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup. Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks’ odds of a road win. They’d all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter. Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers’ lead to 97-87. The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel’el Ware’s put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee’s deficit to 117-114. The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure. For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

stories.title: Film study: What is the Wizards’ offense missing?
stories.summary: Before Thursday night’s barnburner of a loss to the Pistons in double overtime, the vibes around the Wizards, and their offense in particular, were nearing a free fall. The Wiz have the league’s 26th-ranked offense, even after the onslaught against Detroit. There were, to be sure, positive signals to glean. Alex Sarr …
stories.detailText: WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 12: Tre Johnson #12 of the Washington Wizards handles the ball during the game against the Detroit Pistons on November 12, 2026 at Capital One Arena in Washington, DC. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Stephen Gosling/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Before Thursday night’s barnburner of a loss to the Pistons in double overtime, the vibes around the Wizards, and their offense in particular, were nearing a free fall. The Wiz have the league’s 26th-ranked offense, even after the onslaught against Detroit. There were, to be sure, positive signals to glean. Alex Sarr played by far his best game of the season, knocking down four threes. Trae Young showed more scoring juice, shooting 17 free throws and hitting a buzzer-beater to force OT. Sarr and Anthony Davis connected on a rare lob in overtime. But the underlying issues behind the bricktastic 4-9 start will take longer to solve. The Wizards barely shoot any threes, and miss most of the ones they do try. Only the Bulls have shot a worse percentage from deep so far. With poor spacing and clumsy jumbo lineups, the offense has tilted concerningly toward true Trae Young heliocentrism; Young leads the league in seconds per touch. The Wizards use core actions that make a fair amount of sense for their personnel. They rely on side-to-side movement, hoping to launch Young downhill and create better angles for the pick and roll. Consider this frequent action, with Kyshawn George maneuvering to the wing (pending the much-awaited return of NBA.com’s video clips, I’m using screenshots for now): That’s an Iverson cut, intended to distract the defense and free up a Young-AD pick and roll. When Young starts going downhill, Tre Johnson flies up in tandem from the opposite corner. But the Pacers easily box Young toward the wing and funnel the ball away from the middle: Young makes the pass to AJ Dybantsa, but Pascal Siakam closes him down, and Dybantsa, with no advantage, throws the ball away. This is not an uncommon sight for the Wizards — a Young pick and roll in tight confines near the sideline, putting minimal pressure on the opposing center. The Wizards have to find a way to make plays like this impact the defense more. They’re simply not getting enough out of their secondary actions. Above, for example, Johnson sprinting up from the corner is a good idea in theory. But nobody is screening for Johnson here. What if AD had turned at speed and set a pindown for him, just as the defense expects a screen for Young? The best offenses pivot into second and third actions. These are built-in counters, depending on how the defense guards the initial one. Consider Sarr in this position, after running a pick and pop: Bilal Coulibaly’s cut through the paint is a scripted thing many teams with shooting bigs do. It’s meant to drag away the help defender closest to Sarr — the guy whose job it would be to stunt toward Sarr and contest a three-pointer. But here, Sarr set the screen near half-court and barely made contact. Larry Nance Jr. recovered easily; no rotation needed. This first action didn’t yield much, which is normal. The next step for the Wiz is moving quickly and effectively into something else, and making the right reads from there. This is where the above play ended up: Sarr dribbles into a hand-off with Johnson, who has sprinted into the space that Coulibaly vacated. This looks promising; George is spaced one pass away, and Johnson has his defender on his back. But Johnson doesn’t see the pass to George in time, and Jalen Slawson blows up his dribble for a dunk the other way. They have the right idea here. They’re trying to use Sarr and Johnson in their optimal roles. But defenses see these kinds of actions every game. Without a higher level of precision — physical, well-timed screens, and snappy passing — these plays look ordinary and even aimless. There are ways to loosen this up. Step one, of course, is to make some shots. (Even Thursday was a mixed bag in this regard, with Johnson shooting 1-of-9 from three.) Getting more consistent offense from wings other than George, who is leveling up before our eyes, would be a godsend. Most of all, the Wizards need Young to find more success probing around and behind bigs, rather than ending up in these situations: The Wizards have been focused on running these “angle” pick and rolls near the sideline. They are useful for generating pocket passes to the bigs, while spacing guys on the other side. But too often, with Young struggling to separate off the dribble, opposing teams are using aggressive coverages and pinning Young to the sideline. Tough games are looming against feisty, athletic Western Conference teams in Houston and Memphis. With a 4-9 record, they’ll need to find a way to create more advantages in short order.

stories.title: D’Angelo Russell and LaMelo Ball: Darling vs. Discarded
stories.summary: LaMelo Ball and D’Angelo Russell are locked together as Wolves point guards who were thought to be the future.
stories.detailText: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - NOVEMBER 12: The back of LaMelo Ball #1 of the Minnesota Timberwolves jersey during the game against the Dallas Mavericks on November 12, 2026 at Target Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by David Sherman/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Just a few years ago, the Minnesota Timberwolves made a deal for an enigmatic, polarizing point guard using a first-round pick and a franchise legend (do not disrespect Andrew Wiggins, that’s my guy), just as they did in this offseason. The Wolves were universally lambasted for this move, with their trade partner being praised for selling high. D’Angelo Russell is one of the most reviled Wolves of recent history. Despite a few decent years (or months), his turnovers, early shot-clock off-the-dribble threes, and miserable defense led to a benching in the playoffs against the Memphis Grizzlies for Jordan McLaughlin, and his reputation with the fanbase never really recovered. Maybe it’s partly that Russell was the outgoing piece on one of the best trades the Wolves franchise have ever pulled off that made him so infinitely laugh-at-able for fans. Still, Russell’s first few months in a Wolves jersey ahead of the COVID lockdown were like lightning in a bottle. Those same fans who now laugh at him were celebrating what he brought to the team in a season that began with Treveon Graham in the starting lineup. That feels a lot like Wolves fans clamoring for LaMelo Ball as a second star who brings joy instead of moodiness and moroseness. LaMelo Ball has now amassed 223 points & 75 assists in his first 12 games w/the Wolves.
