He is just the 2nd player in @Timberwolves history to record 200+ points & 75+ assists in their first 12 games w/ the franchise (D'Angelo Russell: 260 points/79 assists; 2/10-3/10/2020). pic.twitter.com/ZcCIPIQgBW — Timberwolves PR (@Twolves_PR) November 13, 2026 But the question then becomes a sad one of whether caution is necessary at a time that is so full of joy. Despite the absence of Anthony Edwards, the Timberwolves are on a five-game win streak on the shoulders of Ball. After multiple years of joyless, winning basketball, the Wolves have their heart back. So is that question even worth asking? Is this piece worth writing? The obvious answer is no. The big difference in LaMelo Ball and D’Angelo Russell’s first 12 games for the Wolves is that Minnesota has gone 9-3 with Ball at the helm, an equal reflection of Russell’s 3-9. And yes, the team around these players was far worse in the 2019-20 season than it is now, but still, Minnesota is winning with one young star point guard leading the charge, when his apparent predecessor couldn’t do so. To add to it, the view of the trade is so vastly different already this season. The Golden State Warriors traded Russell, Omari Spellman, and Jacob Evans III for Andrew Wiggins and a top-3 protected first-round pick, which eventually landed at seventh overall and became Jonathan Kuminga (hey, look at that!). Even within that lightning stretch from Russell, Wiggins was playing incredibly well next to Steph Curry. When the draft lottery arrived a few months later, the Wolves landed Anthony Edwards at first-overall, the Warriors took James Wiseman (which was always a bad choice), and the Charlotte Hornets took Ball. The Warriors would go on to win a title with Wiggins taking his play to another level as the clear second option on offense and an absolutely rabid rebounder, while Russell was quickly downgraded to the third option for a team that was still bottom-10 in the NBA. That certainly played a part. But now, Naz Reid is miserable in Charlotte, the first rounder the Wolves sent the Hornets is seven years out and completely out of mind, and Ball is playing his way into an All-Star – dare I say an All-NBA – nod. The perception is entirely opposite, which means that any step back will hurt so much more. Wolves fans have bought in, they’ve signed up, they’ve gone to war for this player and this team in a way they hadn’t, because the night-to-night performances are consistent and fun. I mean, honestly, we went so hard at an online NBA analyst that he went on a Wolves podcast, got succinctly disproven, and was successfully converted into a believer. Today's show w/ @HPbasketball – How do we assess teams effectively this early in the season? – Looking "under the hood" at the Wolves' defense and offense – Running my Jonathan Kuminga-Aaron Gordon player comp by someone who watched Gordon's integration to Denver up close – Me… pic.twitter.com/DfFLhKfk3h — Dane Moore (@DaneMooreNBA) November 11, 2026 So why can’t I shake the feeling of deja vu, that feeling that maybe the Wolves’ new star point guard has what it takes to take the Wolves out of the plateau they’ve been at, one that was eventually only half paid off with Russell. Ball has been more than a dream outcome so far this season. Reid, as beloved as he was, was always a low price to pay for the guy who was bringing Moussa Diabate into Amare Stoudemire conversations in the context of the Hornets playing to the statistical level of the Run-and-Gun Phoenix Suns. Minnesota got a 6’7 orchestrator and offensive maestro for pennies on the dollar, which is not what they gave up for Russell. I guess the answer is the same one that I came to in 2020, when Minnesota finished with one of the worst records in the league. While stuck in lockdown, longing for some Wolves basketball, I would hang around and watch the same “Track the Pack” episode welcoming Russell to Minnesota, followed by highlight after highlight of the Malik Beasley, D’Angelo Russell, and Jarred Vanderbilt Wolves. I chose to enjoy it then. I choose to enjoy this now. Hopefully, this version of Ball is more real than those first 12 games of Russell were. Hopefully, Minnesota keeps winning behind their point guard of the future. Hopefully, Anthony Edwards returns to an offensive ecosystem that has survived without him, but reaches a new level with him. Hopefully, this team can win it all. But, in the meantime, let’s enjoy the team that exists, and remember that comparisons and contrasts do not always come from a place of sad disrespect. Let’s enjoy this, Wolves fans. Fun doesn’t always last, but it’s certainly better now than it has been in years. Maybe, just maybe, the most fun since that 12-game stretch where Minnesota and fans were sure they had found their joy in D’Angelo Russell.

stories.title: Rockets fourth-quarter three-point shooting has been clutch
stories.summary: The Rockets have improved on a weak point from last year.
stories.detailText: HOUSTON, TX - NOVEMBER 13: Fred VanVleet #5 of the Houston Rockets shoots the ball during the game against the Utah Jazz during a 2026 Emirates NBA Cup game on November 13, 2026 at the Toyota Center in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Logan Riely/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images After their first two-game losing streak of the season, where the Houston Rockets suffered losses to the Dallas Mavericks and Phoenix Suns, the Rockets have quickly righted the ship, and after a suprisingly hard fought win over the Utah Jazz, the Rockets have now won three straight and are 10-3 on the season. Alperen Sengun finished with the second-most points in a game in his career, carrying the Rockets with 43 points. The Rockets relinquished a 12-point lead early in the third quarter as the 1-11 Jazz actually took the lead at one point. The Rockets and Jazz traded blows for most of the third quarter, leading into the fourth. In the fourth quarter, Sengun continued his dominance, controlling the game. Of course, his play had a lot to do with the Rockets’ win, but another area that the Rockets have excelled at all season also played a big part. The Rockets entered the game as the league leaders in fourth-quarter three-point shooting. Rockets three-point shooting has helped them put away games in the fourth quarter The Rockets have been one of the best three-point shooting teams all season, coming into Friday’s game ranked seventh overall from downtown at 37.4 percent. Some games are over early when one team dominates the other, and the result is never in doubt, but a lot of games come down to the last few minutes and become back-and-forth contests. That is why the Rockets’ league-leading fourth-quarter three-point shooting is so important. Several times this season, the Rockets have made multiple shots from downtown in a row in the final period, which completely shifts the momentum in a close game. The Rockets have seen their fourth-quarter three-point shooting improve over the last three seasons. In the 2024-25 season, the Rockets were bottom five in this category; last season, they improved to tenth, and this season, they are the best in the league. That happened again in Friday’s win, as Bogdan Bogdanović and Kevin Durant each hit a huge three-pointer, with the Jazz cutting the lead to one late in the fourth quarter. The Rockets’ fourth-quarter shooting matters in close regular-season games, but especially in high-pressure playoff games, and could be the difference between another first-round exit and the Rockets’ first deep playoff run since the 2017-18 season.

stories.title: Josh Hart searching for answers after zero-point outing in Knicks loss
stories.summary: Knicks wing Josh Hart said he is "not in a good headspace" after he was held scoreless and benched for the fourth quarter of Friday's 106-104 NBA Cup loss to the Pacers.
stories.detailText: New York Knicks wing Josh Hart said he is "not in a good headspace" after he was held scoreless and benched for the fourth quarter of Friday's 106-104 NBA Cup loss to the Indiana Pacers . Hart is averaging a career-low 7.3 points per game early in the season as he has been hampered a sore ankle and illness. He hasn't scored more than 10 points since Oct. 25 -- a six-game stretch for him -- and was 0-for-4 from the field against the Pacers. "Wish I could tell you," Hart told reporters about how he could fix his issues. "Don't know. Right now I'm not in a good headspace, and I got to figure out how to improve that and improve my play." Hart is one of three Knicks players off to notably slow starts. Mikal Bridges , who was benched in previous games, found a rhythm by going 8-for-12 for 18 points against the Pacers, while OG Anunoby languished through another 4-for-13 night, telling reporters he's "not sure" why he is struggling to make baskets near the rim. Hart had hoped to reach an extension with the Knicks before the season, but New York announced Oct. 9 that it was tabling all contract talks with Hart and Karl-Anthony Towns . Friday's loss dropped the defending champions to 6-6. "Just have to be better," Hart told reporters after Friday's game. "Have to be better mentally. I just gotta get my mental right."

stories.title: Phoenix might be figuring things out, one stop at a time
stories.summary: The Suns still have plenty of problems, but their recent defensive improvement is worth celebrating.
stories.detailText: PHOENIX, AZ - NOVEMBER 12: Miles Bridges #22 and Jordan Goodwin #23 of the Phoenix Suns touch fingers after the game against the Charlotte Hornets on November 12, 2026 at Mortgage Matchup Center in Phoenix, Arizona. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Barry Gossage/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Need a little hope? Looking for something to give you those warm and fuzzies as you sip your morning coffee? The sugar and cream aren’t doing enough to brighten your day? Well, for all the ugly statistics we’ve been compiling about the Phoenix Suns lately, here’s one that might make that coffee taste a little sweeter. Through the first six games of the regular season, Phoenix ranked dead last in the NBA in defensive rating, surrendering a staggering 124.5 points per 100 possessions. It was an atrocious start, one that had us questioning whether this team possessed the personnel, discipline, or defensive identity necessary to compete night in and night out. But since then? Things have changed considerably. Over their last five games, the Suns have posted a defensive rating of 109.0, the sixth-best mark in the NBA during that stretch. Their net rating has climbed to +4.2, ranking ninth in the league, a significant improvement from the -10.3 net rating that placed them 25th during their first six games. The Suns’ defensive turnaround is worth noting. First 6 games: 124.5 DRTG (30th) -10.3 NET (25th) Since then: 109.0 DRTG (6th) +4.2 NET (9th) That’s a 15.5-point improvement in defensive rating. pic.twitter.com/7G5HGB6wrz — John Voita, III (@DarthVoita) November 13, 2026 That’s a pretty substantial turnaround in a relatively short period of time. And perhaps the most encouraging part is that those numbers include the absolute shellacking Phoenix suffered at the hands of the Spurs . Even with that disaster factored into the equation, the Suns have managed to establish themselves as one of the league’s more effective defensive teams over their last five outings. Now, does that mean all their problems have magically disappeared? Of course not. The rebounding remains atrocious, the lack of size continues to create significant disadvantages, and the questions surrounding roster construction and player fit aren’t going anywhere anytime soon. But there is something encouraging about watching this team begin to stabilize defensively. Much like last season, Phoenix stumbled out of the gate, struggling to establish any semblance of consistency before gradually finding its footing. And while we’re still dealing with a relatively small sample size, the defensive improvement suggests that some of the early growing pains are beginning to subside. The rotations are becoming more connected. The effort is more consistent. And the Suns are beginning to demonstrate they can make life difficult for opposing offenses, despite the physical limitations that continue to plague this roster. There’s still plenty of work to be done, and nobody should be throwing a parade over five games of improved defensive efficiency. But considering where this team stood after six games, seeing Phoenix climb from the league’s worst defensive rating to the sixth-best over its next five is certainly worth acknowledging. The defense is giving us something to feel good about. Perhaps it’s a reminder that sometimes these things take time. I’ll be the first to admit that I’m guilty of overreacting. I constantly find myself mining statistics, searching for numbers that either validate what I’m witnessing while watching these basketball games or challenge the conclusions I’ve already started forming. That’s always the fascinating part of analyzing sports. There’s the eye test, there’s the data test, and somewhere in between lies the reality of what’s actually happening on the court. And sometimes, multiple things can be true simultaneously. The Phoenix Suns can be atrocious on the boards while still developing into a good defensive team. Those two realities aren’t mutually exclusive, and we’re beginning to see evidence of that as Phoenix demonstrates an improved ability to shut down opposing offenses for extended stretches, creating enough separation to secure victories. The issues with rim deterrence remain, and opposing teams continue to exploit the Suns’ lack of size around the basket. But on the perimeter? Things are beginning to look considerably better. Through the first six games of the season, Phoenix was allowing opponents to shoot 40.3% from beyond the arc, the second-worst mark in the NBA. It was a troubling statistic that reflected a defense struggling with rotations, communication, and the ability to consistently contest shots. Since then, that number has dropped to 33.9%, the 10th-best mark in the league during a five-game stretch in which the Suns have gone 4-1. Part of it can certainly be attributed to regression toward the mean. Opponents were unlikely to continue shooting above 40% from deep indefinitely. But dismissing the entire improvement as statistical normalization would overlook the tangible progress we’re witnessing from Phoenix defensively. The individual numbers help illustrate that improvement. During the first six games, opponents were shooting 46.7% from three against Dillon Brooks. Over the last five, that number has dropped to 37.7%. Still not particularly impressive, but considerably better than what we witnessed during the opening stretch. Miles Bridges, who appeared lost on more than a few defensive rotations early in the season, has experienced a similar improvement. Opponents were shooting 38.1% from beyond the arc against him during the first six games. That number has since fallen to 34.7%. These aren’t insignificant developments. They’re signs of players beginning to understand their responsibilities, recognize rotations, and operate with greater cohesion within Jordan Ott’s defensive system. There’s another factor contributing to the increased defensive intensity. The bench. Jordan Goodwin has been fantastic over the last two games, bringing the kind of relentless energy and defensive aggression that can completely alter the complexion of a basketball game. Ryan Dunn has also begun making a more noticeable impact, using his length, athleticism, and defensive instincts to disrupt opposing offenses. Together, they’ve helped give Phoenix something that was desperately missing during the early portion of the season: a second unit capable of changing the momentum of a game through defensive effort. The numbers reflect that impact. Through the first six games, the Suns’ bench posted a net rating of +1.5. Over the last five games, that number has improved to +5.3. That’s meaningful progress, particularly for a team whose starting lineup continues to struggle with consistency and finding the right combinations. The bench has become a catalyst for much of the Suns’ recent success, providing the defensive intensity, cohesion, and energy that have helped stabilize a team that looked completely disjointed at the start of the season. Does five games of improved defensive performance mean Phoenix has solved all its problems? Certainly not. The rebounding remains a disaster, the interior defense still needs significant attention, and the roster continues to present challenges that aren’t going to disappear overnight. But perhaps that’s the lesson here. As much as we want immediate answers, as much as we want the statistics to confirm our suspicions after every game, sometimes a team needs time to figure out how its pieces fit together. While the Suns are still a work in progress, the defensive numbers suggest that some of those pieces are finally beginning to fall into place. So go ahead. Take another sip of that coffee.

stories.title: Josh Hart admits he’s ‘not in a good head space’ as his Knicks struggles mount
stories.summary: Josh Hart’s issues aren’t exclusive to his shot.
stories.detailText: Josh Hart Knicks INDIANAPOLIS — Josh Hart’s issues aren’t exclusive to his shot . The Knicks veteran said he’s mentally struggling to start a disappointing season, and he doesn’t know how to break out of it. “Wish I could tell you,” Hart said. “Don’t know. Right now I’m not in a good head space and I got to figure out how to improve that. And improve my play.” Asked what that meant, Hart, who is shooting just 36 percent on the season, said, “Just mentally. Got to be better mentally. Got to figure stuff out.” Josh Hart of the New York Knicks shoots a 3-pointer against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images Hart finished scoreless Friday night and was benched for the entire fourth quarter of a 106-104 loss to the Pacers , among the low points of a season that has never been on track for the 31-year-old. He’s up for an extension, but the Knicks put out a statement in October declaring they’re shutting down all negotiations, including Hart’s and Karl-Anthony Towns’. Hart revealed Friday that he suffered a calf injury before training camp, which set back his conditioning. He then hurt his ankle and missed three games. Part of the issue is the roster. The Knicks are stacked with wings and guards, creating congestion and sporadic playing time. Mikal Bridges has also been benched , as coach Mike Brown leaned on Landry Shamet and Miles McBride. Brown acknowledged that finding time for Bridges and Hart could be difficult. Josh Hart, left, speaks with New York Knicks teammate Mikal Bridges during a game against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images “There are several different ways you can look at it,” Hart said. “You can look at it, if they have it going, cool. Good. You could look at it like, ‘OK, maybe something else has to change.’” Hart didn’t specify the “change,” but logic indicates he meant a trade. Three years ago, Leon Rose faced a similar conundrum. Too many guards, not enough minutes. So Rose traded two — RJ Barrett and Immanuel Quickley — for a bigger forward in OG Anunoby. Beginning Sunday, the Knicks face Barrett and Quickley twice in three days in Toronto, while Hart tries to find a better headspace.

stories.title: Draymond Green defends Rockets from ‘dirty' label after Steph Curry injury
stories.summary: Draymond Green took the initiative of defending the Houston Rockets from their 'dirty' label following Steph Curry's injury during their clash.
stories.detailText: Draymond Green defends Rockets from ‘dirty' label after Steph Curry injury originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area Draymond Green does not think the Houston Rockets are a dirty team. He does, however, believe they are a very physical one. Speaking on “The Draymond Green Show” as he discussed Steph Curry’s injury and playing without him, Green addressed the label that followed the Warriors’ 115-108 loss in Houston on Nov. 11. Curry grimaced and reached for his right side after tangling with Rockets center Alperen Sengun on a screen early in the first quarter, leaving the game minutes later. An MRI confirmed an oblique abdominal tear, and Curry will be re-evaluated in two weeks, with ESPN’s Shams Charania reporting the team expects him to miss closer to a month. Some fans blamed Sengun, yet Green explains the team is just outright physical, not dirty. “I know a lot of people are saying, ‘Oh man, the Houston Rockets are a dirty team.’ I don’t get off into that dirty thing,” Green said. “Every now and then you see some people that just do things that are downright dirty, and it happens, and when it does, I’ll speak on it.” The matchup has been physical before. Curry left a Warriors loss to Houston last November with a right quad contusion after a collision with Amen Thompson and a screen by Sengun. Wednesday’s game saw Rockets guard Marcus Smart ejected for throwing a punch that grazed the nose of Warriors center Charles Bassey, and the NBA suspended Smart three games. Bassey said Smart was playing dirty “the whole game” and called the punch “fake toughness.” Green drew a different line. He said the thing that bothers him most about Houston is not rough play. “Do they do some bulls— when we play them? Absolutely,” Green said. “I think the thing that may irritate me the most is, like, they play super physical, but then they start flopping sometimes, you know. And so I would say that irritates me more, but I’m not going to sit here and call them a dirty team. They’re a physical team.” Green said the film backs it up. “When we were watching film pregame, you can see on the film they are physical as hell, and so give them credit,” Green said. Green will speak up when something truly is dirty. In his eyes, the Rockets are just physical Download and follow the Dubs Talk Podcast

stories.title: FAA ground stop throws sports world into travel chaos ahead of weekend games
stories.summary: Travel plans for teams in multiple sports were disrupted by the FAA's nationwide ground stop of all flights because of communications problems.
stories.detailText: The Federal Aviation Administration's decision to ground all flights nationwide for several hours Friday threw the sports world into chaos, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams scrambling to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend. The ground stop lasted more than four hours before the FAA announced Friday evening that airplane departures could resume. Transportation officials cited "extraordinary circumstances" caused by communications issues at regional air traffic control centers for the stoppage. Some professional sports teams were searching for hotel rooms, college teams were left to reschedule flights, and some teams had even taken the extraordinary step of chartering buses rather than waiting for the ground stop to end. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy even encouraged NCAA football teams to reach out to the FAA so the agency could help prioritize flights for Saturday's games as more than 2,500 flights were canceled nationwide with hundreds more being delayed. Most college football teams playing Saturday travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left many schools -- including No. 2 Utah , No. 8 Texas and No. 9 Tennessee -- at a standstill as they departed for road games. The Utes play at No. 22 Arizona , the Longhorns visit No. 24 LSU , and the Volunteers are traveling to Texas A&M in three of the bigger games of the weekend. Texas and Tennessee returned to their campuses during the ground stoppage. Once it was lifted after more than four hours of uncertainty, the schools began making plans to fly out as soon as possible. They each landed at their respective destinations late Friday night. No. 19 Ole Miss did not travel Friday night to Oklahoma , and the SEC announced that their game would be moved to Sunday at 1 p.m. ET. Auburn took buses to Mississippi State , and the start time for their game was moved from noon ET to 4:15 p.m. Purdue took buses from West Lafayette, Indiana, for its game at No. 15 Iowa . In the Big 12, the kickoff time for Kansas at West Virginia was moved to 3:30 p.m. ET. Arizona State , which deplaned and headed home to rest during Friday's ground stop, planned to fly to Orlando, Florida, on Saturday. The Sun Devils' game against the UCF Knights , originally scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. ET, was moved to 5:30 p.m. Baylor 's game at No. 10 BYU was rescheduled to 7 p.m. ET. ESPN also confirmed that Oregon State , which is scheduled to play at No. 24 Boise State on Saturday (6 p.m. ET), initially began traveling to Idaho by bus before heading back to the airport Friday evening. The Beavers boarded an airplane later Friday for their trip to Boise. Other teams from the Group of 6 conferences that were grounded include Wyoming (at UTEP ) and Colorado State , whose players were shown holding a walk-through at Northern Colorado Regional Airport as they waited to depart to play Washington State . Tulane , which was scheduled to fly to Houston for its game against Rice on Saturday, was set to board five buses to make the 350-mile drive Friday night. Other schools affected by the stoppage included Washington , Kansas State and Minnesota . Washington spokesperson Kurt Svoboda said the Huskies returned to campus when flights were grounded, but officials stayed in touch with their Alaska/Hawaiian Airlines partners and their flight crew remained in place. The Huskies planned to fly out late Friday. On Friday night, Florida State was playing at Pittsburgh , Illinois was visiting fourth-ranked UCLA , and No. 14 Houston was visiting Colorado . Those teams were hoping their charter flights home afterward would be unaffected by the upheaval. It also was unclear whether any referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would have trouble making it. The Big Ten said in a statement that all of its officials had arrived for their scheduled assignments Saturday. Several teams took off before the stoppage began, including all of those traveling in the ACC; Missouri , which was flying to top-ranked Georgia ; Duke , which was visiting fifth-ranked Miami ; and No. 10 Texas Tech , which posted on social media images of its arrival for a game at Oklahoma State . NFL teams playing Sunday typically travel the day before their games, and they were expected to fly as planned Saturday. Meanwhile, the Brooklyn Nets were among five NBA teams scheduled to fly Friday for games Saturday. They had just boarded the team plane in New Orleans after playing the Pelicans earlier this week when their flight to Memphis was halted in place. The Detroit Pistons flew earlier in the day to Miami. The Cleveland Cavaliers , Chicago Bulls and Memphis Grizzlies played Friday night and were due to fly afterward. The Cavaliers played in Miami on Friday night and were scheduled to play the Dallas Mavericks at home Saturday. Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson said about 90 minutes before tipoff that his team was scrambling to find hotel rooms for Friday night. The team ultimately decided to stay the night and leave for Dallas at 9 a.m. Saturday. "It's part of it. You just adapt," Atkinson said. There are 14 scheduled games in the NHL on Saturday. The Florida Panthers were among the majority that made it to their destinations before the stoppage, but the Sharks were left waiting in San Jose to see whether they would be able to travel to Utah . JuJu Watkins and her third-ranked USC teammates were trying to get to South Carolina for their basketball game Sunday against the top-ranked Gamecocks. The team had just boarded its flight at Los Angeles International Airport when the ground stop was issued. After a while, the decision was made to deboard passengers, and the team returned to the Galen Center. In soccer, the Utah Royals were already in the Washington, D.C., area ahead of their National Women's Soccer League semifinal against the Washington Spirit on Saturday. But the Kansas City Current were supposed to depart Friday for their semifinal against Gotham FC on Sunday in New York, and team officials were uncertain when their flight would be allowed to leave. The U.S. men's national team's match against Haiti on Saturday in Miami was unaffected by the ground stop. Both teams and officials already were in town for the first leg of the two-match CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinal series. ESPN's Mark Schlabach, Pete Thamel, Adam Rittenberg and Andrea Adelson and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.title: Hawks unable to outlast Bulls in overtime loss
stories.summary: A disappointing loss for the Hawks in the NBA Cup.
stories.detailText: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 13: Jalen Smith #25 of the Chicago Bulls and Onyeka Okongwu #17 of the Atlanta Hawks jump at tip off during the first half of the Emirates NBA Cup game at the United Center on November 13, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Daniel Bartel/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Atlanta Hawks were in action in the NBA Cup on Friday night but came up short in a 125-117 road loss in overtime against the Chicago Bulls. Jalen Johnson registered a triple-double of 27 points, 11 rebounds, and 10 assists and CJ McCollum added 20 points off the bench. For the Bulls — without star rookie Caleb Wilson — Norman Powell led the way with 33 points with seven Bulls scoring in double-digits. The Hawks would have entered this game as favorites, with the Bulls heading into this game on the back of an eight-game losing streak and looking for just their second win of the season. Without impressive rookie Caleb Wilson, the Bulls were missing talent that is sorely needed and handed the Hawks a significant advantage with his absence. In reality, that is not how it played out. The Hawks’ time spent leading this game was extremely brief, and it was the Bulls who ran out to a double-digit lead in the first quarter behind 10 first quarter points from Powell. The key difference in this game began to become clear from the first quarter as the Hawks shot 2-of-8 from three-point range as the visitors’ struggles shooting the ball became more concrete in the second quarter. The Bulls, meanwhile, had no problem dispatching their three-pointers and began to run their lead to a game-high 18 points in the second quarter. While the Hawks found some success in the paint — and this was how they began to reign in the Chicago lead — the three-point shooting story was becoming clear: 3-of-17 for Atlanta, while the Bulls shot 11-of-28 from three in the first half. The Hawks were, at times, settling for transition, pull-up threes from above the break but only shot 1-of-11 from such shots in this game: Off of a miss, Nickeil Alexander-Walker pushes the ball up the floor and springs into a three-pointer, but cannot convert: View Link Off of the pass from Dyson Daniels, Johnson pulls up into a three-pointer which is missed: View Link On this attempt, the Hawks work themselves into a better opportunity from above the break, with Alexander-Walker finding Daniels, who finds Onyeka Okongwu all alone above the break, but the three is missed: View Link The Hawks would continue to strike out on these opportunities all night long, and relied on the inside scoring of Johnson, and some tough, crafty baskets from McCollum to keep the visitors in range, even tying the game in late stages of the third quarter. The Bulls, however, quickly stretched their lead back to 10 in the fourth quarter, giving the Hawks a lot of work to do on the road. Even with 2:22 remaining the Hawks faced an uphill battle of seven points, but Okongwu and Johnson, tied the game. Having not led the game since the first quarter — when the game was 7-6 — the Hawks had multiple opportunities to take a late lead in this game. The first comes in the form of the Hawks failing to secure a rebound off of a missed shot from Jalen Smith, with Johnson losing the rebound and the Bulls get the opportunity to call a timeout: View Link After a missed shot from Powell inside, the Hawks get a chance to get out in transition. Johnson is faced by Josh Giddey, and elects to pass the ball back out to the perimeter to Alexander-Walker, who is unable to hit the three-pointer: View Link I’m not sure Johnson realized how strong his advantage was here: no help was coming, Giddey was on his own, and it’s a one-on-one near the rim you would heavily back Johnson to score or draw a foul. Instead, he makes the unselfish play and finds Alexander-Walker, who continued his unfortunate shooting trend in this game at the wrong time. The Hawks would get another chance as they advance the ball off of a timeout after another Bulls miss. Okongwu delivers a good pass to the cutting Aaron Wiggins, who is surely rim-side and through for a layup, but cannot complete the catch as the ball slips through his fingers and out of play: View Link Three differing chances for the Hawks to get/to score and all of them passed them by, and the game goes to overtime. The Hawks would take their first lead since the first quarter, but it would not last, as Powell scored nine points in the overtime period to pull away from the Hawks before a dagger three Matas Buzelis dashes any hopes of a Hawks victory. Postgame, Hawks head coach Quin Snyder highlighted the start of the game as an issue for the Hawks and discussed how the Hawks’ shooting issues were exacerbated by the Bulls’ own good three-point shooting night. “We didn’t play with the force at the beginning of the game,” said Snyder postgame. “That impacts our defense, it’s, kind of, the complimentary of basketball: how your defense affects your offense. When we’re not forceful defensively, or active, and we’re not running. We know the things we need to have in the front of our minds to focus on. When we don’t do that, we don’t play well. By the same token, we started to find that, 18 (points) down. When you’re not shooting the ball well — we had a bad shooting night, which is going to happen — those things become even more important. When your opponent is shooting the ball, it compounds itself. We take from it what we can, and there’s a lot here we can focus on.” “We’ve got to come out with energy from the jump, we just didn’t do that,” added Jalen Johnson. This game can be summed up by living by the three and dying by the three. The Hawks finished with 8-of-40 from three (20%) while the Bulls shot 20-of-50 from three (40%), and while there are other nuances of this game that did not go the Hawks’ way (which we’ll touch on in a moment), the game can really be summed up as simply as that. If you hit eight threes while your opponent hits 20 (a 60-24 point disparity) it’s difficult to win games consistently. The fact the Hawks almost did, speaks to the nature of the Bulls’ season (allowing Jalen Smith to 15 shots and 1-of-6 from three is something the Bulls allowed to happen, for some reason). From the Hawks’ side, it was another difficult night shooting the three from Alexander-Walker, who shot 1-of-11 from three, and 6-of-19 from the field — it just wasn’t his night, and there’s been a couple of those this season where it becomes evident it may not be his night from three and he ends up with a poor percentage on a high volume. It was the same story across the board: reliable three-point shooters for the Hawks couldn’t get their shots to fall. Okongwu shot 2-of-7 from three, while Aaron Wiggins shot 1-of-6 from distance. Turnovers were also a key feature in this game, with the Hawks committing 17 in total, off of which the Bulls scored 20 points. These turnovers, as Snyder often references along with getting stops, impact the Hawks’ ability to establish their identity: it’s key for Atlanta to get out on the run in transition/off of a miss and when the Hawks are committing turnovers this impacts the Hawks significantly. “It’s hard to stop the ball when you turn the ball over,” said CJ McCollum postgame. Chicago turnovers were also how the Hawks remained in this game, scoring 34 points off of the Bulls’ 24 turnovers — without these, the Hawks would not have been able to close the margin as they did, with Johnson and McCollum credited for 10 points apiece off of Chicago turnovers. In addition, when the Hawks are off form from three, they are at least able to rack up points in the paint — many of which came off of turnovers — scoring 66 points in the paint, with Johnson accounting for 20 of these. Johnson finished with 27 points on 11-of-26 shooting from the field to go with his triple-double. The Hawks were chasing the game for much of the affair, but Snyder didn’t believe that this pursuit tired the Hawks physically. “I didn’t feel like we were tired,” said Snyder. “Powell hit some tough shots in the overtime which I thought we defended pretty well. We made a couple of adjustments that our guys executed that I thought were really good. You put yourself in a position where you’ve got to make a lot of plays. We made enough to go to get where we were, but the game goes back and forth, and it went back one too many times.” There’s no doubt the Hawks left themselves with a lot of work to do, both in the first half and in the fourth quarter when they trailed by double-digits. But they had their chances in regulation, and it slipped through their fingers (well, quite literally in Wiggins’ case). In overtime, the quality of Powell (33 points on 12-of-29 shooting) shone through as he seized the game, with enough support from the rest to see the Bulls through. It’s a poor loss for the Hawks, who would have won this game had they hit any number of their 26 missed threes in regulation. They were also off since Monday, while the Bulls were in action on Wednesday, so their flat start to the game looks worse with context. In the context of the NBA Cup, the Hawks still have a positive point differential and are still in play to advance but cannot afford another loss such as this. The Hawks (7-6) are back in action on Sunday when they will encounter another team on the road desperate for victory: the 1-12 Milwaukee Bucks. Until next time!

stories.title: Bucks Reacts Survey Results: When it come to the Giannis trade, fans are on the fence
stories.summary: There’s very little end-stopping here—Bucks fans are enjambed on the trade-verdict fence.
stories.detailText: SALT LAKE CITY, UT - NOVEMBER 10: Giannis Antetokounmpo #7 of the Miami Heat smiles during the game against the Utah Jazz on November 10, 2026 at Delta Center in Salt Lake City, Utah. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Alex Goodlett/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images This week, we revisited the biggest trade in franchise history (sorry, Mr Abdul-Jabbar), taking in early-season results, player form, and respective end-goals to try and determine who, if either team, won the transaction that sent Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis to the Miami Heat in exchange for Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel’el Ware, Kasparas Jakučionis, and picks, including what ended up being Nate Ament. As it stands, fans had plenty to say but, for now at least, are happily straddling the fence. Sir, can I have an extension? The prevailing response (57%) was that it’s simply too early to come to any definitive conclusion regarding the trade. There are, however, plenty of concerns to keep Bucks fans from sleeping easy at night: Regarding the Bucks’ upcoming free agents, I’m right there with you, naveed. But the way things are going , they might just have to pony up to retain every bit of talent they can. No winners, just losers While the majority of voters need more time to tell, 23% are leaning negative, believing Milwaukee did not win the trade. Oh, and Jon Horst is the worst: Can someone check on PackofBrewss88? Also, if the veteran Heat get time to gel, surely the Bucks do too? On another note, there was a larger sentiment that neither team really won the deal: But, hey, as the adage goes, if neither team is happy, then maybe it was a fair trade after all? One foot on the other side While most thought it was too early to tell and 23% leaned negative, a nearly-equal 20% of voters have found their footing on the other side of the fence, feeling the Bucks did , in fact, win the trade. However, as MKE said, it all came—and comes—down to (hard luck and) circumstance: Talk later? Overall, whether fans saw the Bucks as winners, losers, or something in between, a prominent throughline was that this question needs to be revisited later in the year—and beyond: Consider it bookmarked. And on that note, we’re done. As always, thanks for your input—and if you’ve got any further thoughts, be sure to drop ‘em below.

(Photo by Ronald Cortes/Getty Images) | Getty Images I was about 12 years old when I realized that there were people in the Dark Ages who had lived amongst the ruins of the Roman Empire. Once a week in my art class (usually on a Friday) we were given free reign to pursue whatever we wanted, so long as it pertained to either the creation or study of art. Being a poor visual artist, I tended to opt for study, and would plop myself into a beanbag chair in the corner of the room with a stack of art books. In the time before the proliferation of google image searches this felt like a revelation, and I spent countless hours pouring through volumes of paintings that I’d otherwise only have seen in a museum. I can still recall the goosebumpy thrill of stumbling into the deeply shadowed chiaroscuro of El Greco, or the eerie moonlit majesty of John Atkinson Grimshaw. But it was a piece by the French Romantic painter Hubert Robert, found in a compendium of work contained in the Philadelphia Museum of Art, that so confounded me that I begged my teacher to make me a photocopy of it. I kept my humble paper copy of ‘ Ruins of a Roman Bath with Washerwomen ’ in a manila folder on my childhood bookshelf for many years. From time to time I would take it out and just stare at it. I couldn’t understand why it had captured me so, but I knew it had something to do with the nature of the situation. If you’ve seen it, you know that it depicts a towering Roman edifice surrounding a once-ornate bathhouse. It’s clear that the architecture is no longer being maintained. The age is visible. There are stones missing. And yet, it’s still so majestic. The ruin itself testifies to the grandeur that came before. The structure is still enormous and strong, and I suspect that one of the first thoughts that anyone has looking at it, is to wonder what it must have looked like at the peak of the empire. If it were just a painting of those ruins, it would be arresting enough as is. But it’s the people the really threw me. Gathered around the edges of the previously opulent pool, are hunched over figures, doing their laundry in the remains of the bathhouse. I had developed quite a real fondness for the subject of history by the age of twelve, but this was something that had never occurred to me. People had continued living in Roman ruins. I suppose some part of my brain had to have registered this, knowing that the Colosseum was still standing, but to me, ruins weren’t a place where people lived . Sure, if they were important enough, maybe someone would build a museum, and people would come to visit them, but the thought of anyone actually living there was astonishing. But people had in fact done that. It’s all over the historical record. They did their best to maintain the plumbing and the roads, and the structures, and just stayed where they were. Crusaders patched and fortified them. Some people carried on as if the Western Empire still existed, awiating a return to glory that never came. Last night I felt that familiar feeling washing over me any time I saw Warriors fans in the crowd, as the Spurs punctured any illusions of a lingering Golden State greatness. It’s one thing to witness the fall of an empire. It’s another thing altogether to keep living there. For a moment (and in spite of Draymond Green’s flagrant antics), I felt a wave of pity wash over me. It quickly turned to empathy with the realization that I too had been there. Thirty points down at the half, with an all-too-clear vision of the future in front of them, these people were still holding on to a return to glory. Maybe not in this game, but to the season as a whole. Steph Curry turns 39 in March. Draymond Green hasn’t been an offensive plus in years. Jimmy Butler is still to return from an ACL injury at an age where recovery is negligible. Promising rookie Yaxel Lendeborg was learning hard lessons about facing the defense of true contenders (he went 1-13), and probably won’t be up to speed in the way that aging squad needs as they approach their 40’s. There’s no young Kawhi Leonard to tie everything together. The sun is setting. Has, realistically, already set. There are still people doing their laundry in the ruins. And who am I to blame them? If not for the arrival of a certain French sensation, I’d probably be right there with them. But it does speak to the difference in approaches from the two franchises. Pursuing longevity, the Popovich/Duncan-era Spurs almost never cashed in all their chips for an all-or-nothing swing at a title. They kept building as they went. And when the end of their run was well and truly visible, they looked at what they had left and tried to repurpose it in a productive way. It’s not terribly dissimilar from what some of those old Roman communities did. Recognizing the end for what it was, the citizens of cities like Avneches, Aosta, and Split began to build their own structures within the confines of the old city walls, utilizing some of the remaining architecture as ready-made stone quarries for their rebuilding efforts, while retaining the meticulously laid-out street grids of their predecessors. There seems to be this idea circulating around the NBA that a rebuild must tear everything down to the absolute studs. That nothing should remain of the previous era. No notion. No mentality. No prolonged eye on the future. But that’s not how the Celtics or Lakers did it. And it’s not how the Spurs have done it, either. Sometimes it’s okay to acknowledge the wisdom of a previous era, while knowing that it’s time to turn the page. Not everything needs to be abandoned. There are some points of expertise that endure throughout the ages. But you can’t just live in the ruins, either, hoping for a lottery ticket to cure all ills, or a glorious return to form. These Spurs aren’t the Spurs of old, and that’s important to acknowledge. They’re building something of their own now, but they’re doing so within the thoughtfully constructed confines of a previous glory, and the result is something that feels both new and familiar. Something as fresh as it is reminiscent. Something as aspirational as it is nostalgic. You can’t just do your laundry in the halls of a fallen kingdom. That’s how you end up losing your shirt. Takeaways I have to say, Harrison Barnes has looked surprisingly spry so far this season. I assumed he would function as emergency depth when he was re-signed, but he look more like the early-season version of himself from last season, before a slump that allowed Julian Champagnie to work his way into the starting lineup. While he’s certainly not a starter anymore, he’s savvy and sharp-shooting enough to serve as the hot hand on nights where Carter Bryant is missing shots and assignment. That probably raises some questions about Bryant at the same time, but it really underscores just how much functional depth the Spurs have right now. It’s also been great seeing Luke Kornet find more of rhythm with the bench unit, after a somewhat concerning opening slate. There’s no way the Spurs win in such a landslide without him stifling their 2nd unit, and that was his 3rd out of the last 4 games with a positive plus/minus, putting him back into the positive in Defensive Wins Shares and Defensive Box Plus/Minus for the season. I still have concerns about the postseason, but it’s nice to see the trend reverse as the Spurs have badly needed it to. And while I’m not sure that Stephon Castle’s outstanding performance is indicative of how the rest of the season is going to go for him, it was an absolute blast of adrenaline to see him shoot the lights out against the Warriors specifically, especially after seeming hesitant over the past stretch of games, with the additional pain of his shot not falling. Still, you can really see why the Spurs are committed to turning him into an off-ball threat, because when that shot is falling, you become almost impossible to handle. Kudos to Mitch for having the good sense to ride the hot hand on a night when Wemby was getting a lot of defensive attention, but it also felt like this would have been a blowout even if Wemby had ridden the pine after the 1st quarter. If this was Castle finding his shot and his confidence, they really might keep trucking on at a 68-win pace. That quite literally changes everything, and bring into question whether or not rotations should even be altered all that much once Tobias Harris makes his debut, barring situational need. Also, I’d just like to note that Keldon Johnson has really become such a patient jack-of-all for the team. It really doesn’t matter who you put him with, he’s going to find the point of need and do his best to fill it. There have been night where his scoring isn’t needed/prioritized, and he just spent his time crashing the boards and giving it his all on defense, and nights where he comes alive on the offensive team when a particularly juicy matchup presents itself, or the team just needs more points. I’m not sure how the Spurs are going to re-sign him with their eyes on the cap and a whole host of contract balancing issues to come, but I’d love to see them do it. He’s not a perfect player by any means, but he’s really become a perfect Spur. Playing You Out – The Theme Song of the Evening: Lighting Crashes by Live

teamStories.detailText: SAN ANTONIO -- In his first game as the primary offensive engine in place of the injured Stephen Curry , Golden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg went 1-of-13 shooting in a 123-85 blowout loss to the San Antonio Spurs on Friday night. "We just lost by like 100," Lendeborg said. "So you know I'm f---ed up mentally right now." Twelve hours earlier, following the team's morning shootaround in San Antonio, Lendeborg expressed an apprehensive excitement about his elevated scoring role in place of Curry, placing his confidence level at a "6 out of 10." "The other four is like, man, am I going to be able to live up to it?" Lendeborg said. "Am I going to be able to help out the team the way I want to? But time will tell." Lendeborg has had a generally spectacular start to his NBA career, averaging 21.7 points and 7.4 rebounds through his first 12 games and generating early Rookie of the Year buzz. He had 37 points in a win over the LA Clippers when Curry rested earlier in the month. But the Clippers aren't the Spurs. The defending Western Conference champions entered on a 10-game win streak and ripped off an 18-0 run to start the game. Lendeborg had two misses and two turnovers in a silent first quarter. He would finish with three points, seven rebounds and three turnovers. "I was flustered the entire game," Lendeborg said. "Couldn't make a damn layup." The Warriors went 10-of-42 shooting with Victor Wembanyama on the floor, 1a 24% conversion rate that is the worst by any team when Wembanyama has been on the court in a game in his career. "Nobody wanted to go into the paint," Lendeborg said. "Nobody wanted to get their shot blocked by him. So we were all just doing some weak-ass floaters. I don't know how many of us work on those. Especially me. I shot like seven of them. I never work on floaters since like [junior college]." Lendeborg said before the game that he planned to shoot a bunch of 3s in an effort to score over the top of Wembanyama, but he attempted only two and missed both. "He's skinnier than me," Lendeborg said. "I just got to go up there and put an elbow in his chest and jump into his body or something. If he blocks it, he blocks it. I can't go up there scared." The loss dropped the Warriors to 8-5. They get two off days before a road trip to play the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday night without Curry, who is out at least two weeks and presumably longer after tearing an oblique in Houston on Wednesday night. "I'm not going to move past this," Lendeborg said. "I don't know about the rest of us. Everybody said throw it out the window. I can't throw a damn thing out the window."

teamStories.title: Victor Wembanyama, Spurs open on 18-0 run, rout Warriors for 11th straight win
teamStories.summary: Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs pounced on the Warriors with an 18-0 opening run and went on to win 123-85.
teamStories.detailText: SAN ANTONIO -- Victor Wembanyama rocked the rim with a reverse jam off a lob tossed by Stephon Castle on Friday night and quickly fired off a four-punch combination into the padded stanchion underneath the basket. Clearly, the beatdown was on against the Golden State Warriors . "I'm ready to put my body on the line for the team if that allows us to win by 40," Wembanyama said. Wembanyama's dunk with 7:31 left in the opening quarter punctuated an 18-0 run to start the game, and the San Antonio Spurs cruised to a 123-85 win over the Warriors in an NBA Cup game. It was the Spurs' largest run to start a game over the past 30 seasons and the largest allowed by Golden State to start a game under coach Steve Kerr. "They were lights-out," Kerr said of the Spurs. "They played a great first five minutes, took it to us. Give them the credit." San Antonio extended its league-best winning streak to 11 games. Warriors leading scorer Stephen Curry sat out because of an oblique abdominal tear that will keep him out of action for at least two weeks. Castle inflicted most of the damage by hitting his first three 3-pointers in the opening quarter and finished with a season-high 32 points in 25 minutes. It was Castle's sixth career regular-season outing with 30-plus points and his eighth when including the postseason. The 22-year-old entered the contest shooting 31.5% from 3-point range this season but caught fire early against Golden State, finishing 5-of-8 from deep to go with six assists, five rebounds and a block. Castle racked up 13 points in the first quarter on 5-of-7 shooting and finished with at least 30 points, five assists and five rebounds in the second-fewest minutes in franchise history. Wembanyama achieved that stat line in 24 minutes in 2023. "He's in the middle of everything," Spurs coach Mitch Johnson said of Castle. "He's an unbelievable impact player. He's never blinked at anything we've asked, never shown any poor body language. He just attacks everything." That included the hobbled Warriors. Throughout the season, teams have sagged off Castle on the perimeter, essentially daring him to shoot. The 2025 NBA Rookie of the Year made the Warriors pay for those tactics and never hesitated along the way. "I think the biggest obstacle I've had was really myself, kind of just getting into my own head sometimes, not taking open shots and forcing worse shots," Castle said. "I think today just coming in with a clear mind, thinking about our defensive stuff, our principles, trying to play the right way, and the basketball gods found me." San Antonio led by as many as 26 points in the first quarter and took a 30-point lead into halftime. The cushion stretched to as many as 43 with less than a minute to play in the third quarter, when Harrison Barnes nailed a 24-footer to put San Antonio ahead 95-52. Kerr called San Antonio "the best team in the league, the hottest team in the league." The Warriors suffered their most lopsided defeat since Jan. 20, 2025, when they lost by 40 to the Boston Celtics . It was the second consecutive game the Warriors failed to hold a lead at any point. "We can beat you in many ways, and our offense isn't really our only offense," Castle said. "Our defense makes a lot of those plays and sparks our runs. We could be having not the greatest shooting night, but showing up on defense is really a nonnegotiable. If we do those things the right way and play our way, eventually teams will start to break down." ESPN's Anthony Slater and ESPN Research contributed to this report.

stories.title: Patriots place RB TreVeyon Henderson on IR with still unexplained illness
stories.summary: The Patriots placed RB TreVeyon Henderson on injured reserve while he deals with an unexplained neurological issue.
stories.detailText: MUNICH -- The New England Patriots placed running back TreVeyon Henderson on injured reserve Saturday, eight days after Henderson said he recently experienced "an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms." Henderson had already been ruled out for Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions at FC Bayern Munich Arena (9:30 a.m. ET, Fox) earlier in the week. He now will miss at least the next four games. Henderson has said that tests have "come back positive and reassuring," and in a social media post said, "the cause of this remains unknown and unexplainable." The Patriots entered the week with just two healthy running backs -- Corey Kiner and Lan Larison -- as starter Rhamondre Stevenson was managing a knee tendon injury sustained in last Sunday's loss to the Green Bay Packers . Stevenson was a limited participant in the Patriots' two practices in Munich, and coach Mike Vrabel said Friday he was feeling "pretty good" when asked to gauge Stevenson's potential availability for the game at that point. Vrabel said the same thing about wide receiver A.J. Brown , who has missed the past two games with a knee flare-up. A potential tipoff that Stevenson could be active for Sunday's game against the Lions came when Saturday's deadline to elevate players from the practice squad passed and the Patriots didn't elevate a running back. Going into a game with just two running backs would be outside the norm, as most teams have at least three. In other roster moves, the Patriots activated center/guard Greg Van Roten and fullback Reggie Gilliam to the active roster from injured reserve and elevated center/guard Andrew Rupcich from the practice squad for Sunday's game.

stories.title: 3 Eagles tidbits coming out of the NFL trade deadline
stories.summary: Notes on Dallas Goedert, Jordan Davis, and more.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Dallas Goedert #88 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs a route during an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images NFL insiders Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport shared an NFL trade deadline notebook on ESPN that featured several mentions of the Philadelphia Eagles. Let’s take a look at those here. 1) Dallas Goedert drew interest from the 49ers, among other teams. Here’s what was said: While the Eagles traded stars in Davis and center Cam Jurgens in the flurry leading up to the deadline, they held off trading another player who was wanted — Dallas Goedert. Sources said several teams inquired about the pass-catching tight end, including the 49ers. But Goedert, 31, never got close to being traded. He remains in Philadelphia and could even re-sign with the Eagles for 2027. Not exactly shocking to see that teams had interest in acquiring him. Goedert is a solid tight end who could make nice contributions to a contending team. At the same time, the Eagles didn’t need to give him away for meager compensation. Especially when accounting for his salary cap ramifications . It’s interesting to see mention of the Eagles potentially keeping Goedert beyond 2026. It felt like the Eagles were close to moving on from him after each of the past two seasons. And he turns 32 in January. Are the two sides really going to do another one-year bandaid contract? Maybe. The only Eagles tight end currently under contract beyond this season is … Eli Stowers. It wouldn’t be very wise for the team to put all of their eggs in the basket of him panning out since the 2026 second-round pick has yet to show promise thus far. 2) The Bills also had interest in Jordan Davis. Here’s what was said: The two teams that were most aggressive in trading for Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis were the Bills and Jaguars, who wound up trading a first- and second-round pick to the Eagles. Interested to know exactly what the Bills were offering for Davis. Nevertheless, seems like there was a bidding war for the Eagles’ interior defender, which helps to explain why Howie Roseman was able to get such a big return from the jags. 3) The Eagles aren’t happy with the Bengals. Here’s what was said: The Eagles were not pleased that the Bengals reneged on their deal for Ebiketie after learning they would lose a third-round compensatory pick […] Understandably so. The Eagles thought they had a done deal with the Bengals to ship out Ebiketie for a 2027 sixth-round pick. Before it became official, however, Cincy realized (thanks to compensatory picks expert Nick Korte) that acquiring Ebiketie would cause him to forfeit the 2027 third-round pick comp pick they were set to earn for losing Trey Hendrickson. While one can understand why the Bengals wanted to back out after realizing their mistake, this failed trade is a pretty bad look for them. I feel like the Bengals owe the Eagles one. Not exactly sure what that looks like but it’s in Cincy’s own interests to maintain healthy working relationships with other NFL general managers.

stories.title: Cowboys vs 49ers: 2 players to buy, 2 to sell against San Francisco
stories.summary: Four Cowboys players who could play a big role on Sunday
stories.detailText: Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys are coming off a narrow win over the Indianapolis Colts, and now the 7-1 San Francisco 49ers are coming to town, bringing one of the league’s most complete rosters and a defense that has consistently given Dallas problems in their recent matchups. There are some opportunities for the Cowboys, particularly with CeeDee Lamb playing at a high level, but there are also some difficult matchups that could expose weaknesses on Dallas’ roster. Here are two players to buy and two to sell ahead of Sunday’s game. Buy: CeeDee Lamb I mean, who else would this list start with? Lamb has been the best player for the Cowboys all season, and there’s no reason to think that Dallas will stop feeding him the ball. Lamb is coming off a monster performance against Indianapolis, hauling in 10 catches for 195 yards and a touchdown on 16 targets. It was his second-highest receiving total in a game during his career. Through nine games, Lamb has 70 receptions for 904 yards and seven touchdowns. He’s already surpassed the 900-yard mark, and his 108 targets lead the Cowboys by a wide margin. The matchup against San Francisco is difficult, but Lamb is the kind of receiver who can change a game regardless of the opponent. With George Pickens possibly missing another week and Dallas dealing with inconsistencies elsewhere the offense, Dak Prescott should continue looking Lamb’s way early and often. The 49ers will undoubtedly have a plan for him, but Lamb’s recent production makes him difficult to leave out of the buyers market. He’s been the Cowboys’ most reliable playmaker overall, and Dallas needs to find ways to get him involved. DAK TD TO CEEDEE FOR 44 YARDS DALvsIND on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/uIIXrKbg2y — NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026 Sell: Dak Prescott At some point, the Cowboys have to figure out how to beat San Francisco, and Dak Prescott has to be a big part of that solution. Unfortunately, his history against the 49ers doesn’t inspire much confidence. Prescott is 2-4 against San Francisco in his career, including an 0-2 record in the playoffs. In those two postseason games, he has thrown for 460 yards, two touchdowns and three interceptions. His most recent regular-season meetings haven’t been much better. He threw three interceptions in the 2023 blowout loss and two more in the 2024 matchup. Across his four regular-season games against San Francisco, Prescott has completed 65.5% of his passes for 875 yards, eight touchdowns and five interceptions. That’s not necessarily disastrous production, but the turnovers have been costly, particularly against a team that knows how to capitalize on mistakes. The 49ers have won four straight meetings against Dallas, and Prescott will have to overcome both that team history and his own struggles against this opponent. San Francisco’s defense is disciplined, physical and capable of making quarterbacks pay for forcing throws. With Fred Warner leading the unit, Prescott will have to be sharp with his reads and decision-making, especially against the blitz, where he has looked terrible this year. Dallas needs a big performance from its quarterback to pull off the upset. Given the history, though, this is a matchup where I’m selling Prescott until he proves otherwise. Another zero blitz look where everyone is running deep routes and no one is in the middle of the field. Dak let's it fly early and takes a big-hit, almost looks like a go ball, but Lamb is running a post. Miscommunication? Bad ball? Still begging someone to ask someone why they… pic.twitter.com/sPycW7qg9y — Connor Livesay (@ConnorNFLDraft) November 9, 2026 Buy: Brevyn Spann-Ford With Jake Ferguson ruled out due to a knee injury, Brevyn Spann-Ford has an opportunity to take on an even bigger role in the Cowboys’ offense. It might not be the most obvious matchup to exploit, but he could be a sneaky contributor against San Francisco. Spann-Ford has caught 15 passes for 130 yards this season, and his role has been growing. Against Indianapolis, he played 55 offensive snaps compared to Ferguson’s 27, catching two of three targets for 20 yards. That workload suggests the Cowboys are already comfortable giving him significant playing time. The 49ers have plenty of defensive talent to account for, and their attention will naturally gravitate toward Lamb and the Cowboys’ other primary playmakers. That could leave opportunities for Spann-Ford underneath or in the middle of the field, particularly if Dallas uses him to help with protection before releasing him into a route. This isn’t a prediction that Spann-Ford is suddenly going to become the focal point of the passing game. Rather, it’s a bet that his increased playing time and the attention paid to Dallas’ other weapons could create a few favorable opportunities. With Ferguson unavailable, the Cowboys need someone else to contribute from the tight end position. Spann-Ford is in a good position to do that. Sell: Jaishawn Barham The Cowboys have indicated that Jaishawn Barham could see an increased workload as injuries continue to pile up on the defensive side of the ball. That’s understandable from a personnel standpoint, but it also creates a potential problem against an offense as versatile as San Francisco’s. Barham had some encouraging moments early in the season, but his limitations have become more apparent as the competition has increased. His playing time has also been limited recently, which makes the prospect of a larger role against the 49ers particularly concerning. San Francisco is exactly the type of opponent that can put a young linebacker in difficult situations. Kyle Shanahan’s offense uses motion, misdirection and mismatches to create space, and open up running lanes. If Dallas gives him more responsibility, San Francisco will have plenty of opportunities to test him. The Cowboys need all the help they can get defensively, but this is a tough week to ask an inconsistent young player to take on a bigger role.

stories.title: What placing TreVeyon Henderson on IR, activating Greg Van Roten and Reggie Gilliam means for the Patriots
stories.summary: The Patriots made three roster moves ahead of their game against the Lions.
stories.detailText: At around 10 p.m. local time in Germany on Saturday, the New England Patriots announced that they have made some changes to their roster . Running back TreVeyon Henderson was headed to injured reserve due to the illness that has kept him out since late October, while fullback Reggie Gilliam and offensive lineman Greg Van Roten were both activated from IR. With the Patriots having entered the weekend at 52 players on their roster, Saturday’s transactions meant that they now have a full complement of players available again. What else do the moves mean, though? Let’s find out. RB TreVeyon Henderson: Placed on IR TreVeyon Henderson taking to social media last Friday already was an ominous sign. In a statement addressing the illness that had kept him out for more than a week at that point, he mentioned that “my strength, coordination, and some of my physical functions” were affected by the “unexpected and unusual medical emergency” he had been dealing with. While there might still have been hope at that point that he would be able to return in a relatively short period of time, Saturday’s move means that that will not be the case. Henderson will be out for at least the next four games, starting with the upcoming contest against the Detroit Lions. Other games he is now slated to miss include matchups with the Chargers, Bills and Vikings. He is eligible to return to practice and off injured reserve ahead of the Patriots’ Week 15 game in Kansas City, even though an obvious question mark hangs over that comeback given the most recent information we have available — information, head coach Mike Vrabel also did not add to this week. “I talk to TreVeyon every day and just like everybody else that’s not available, he’s working hard to get back,” he said on Thursday at the FC Bayern Munich training facility. “When that is I don’t know. I don’t have a timetable, but I love my interactions with him. I love talking with him and seeing how he’s doing.” From a football perspective, Henderson going to IR officially removes the No. 2 running back from the Patriots’ active roster. This leaves the group looking as follows: 53-man roster (3): Rhamondre Stevenson (38), Corey Kiner (9 | KR), Lan Larison (34) Practice squad (1): Terrell Jennings (26) IR (2): Myles Montgomery (39 | season-ending), TreVeyon Henderson (32) Rhamondre Stevenson is the clear top option, something that would not change with Henderson available. He is the Patriots’ most reliable back in all aspects of playing the position, and by far their best pass protector at the position. Still, Henderson as a rotational second option would bring a more dynamic element to the table than the likes of Corey Kiner and Lan Larison. That element is now missing, even though Kiner in particular has had some promising moments as of late and given Stevenson’s unclear outlook — he is questionable with a knee injury — might see increased reps versus Detroit. In addition to the roster perspective, Henderson going to IR also adds to the numbers crunch regarding the return spots. As a reminder, the Patriots had eight of those available at the start of the year but already used five on the likes of wide receivers A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins, offensive tackle Marcus Bryant and the aforementioned Reggie Gilliam and Greg Van Roten. Two of the remaining three are expected to go to a pair of starters, wide receiver Romeo Doubs and left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker. This, in turn, would potentially leave one such spot open for Henderson. Of course, if they were to qualify for the postseason, the Patriots would get two extra IR-return opportunities. FB Reggie Gilliam: Activated to 53-man roster Gilliam went to injured reserve after the Patriots’ Week 4 win over the Bills. He had been dealing with a knee injury entering that contest, and additionally suffered an ankle ailment in that particular game. New England did not have a traditional fullback on the 53-man roster or practice squad at that point, and never added one either since initially losing Gilliam. This also meant that the fullback packages that were used earlier in the season were not further expanded upon, which in turn might have also played its part in the Patriots struggling to consistently move the football on the ground. Gilliam returning will not instantly fix those issues, but he should be an immediate upgrade over the player the team primarily used to replace him, since-released rookie tight end Tanner Arkin. At the very least, the Patriots can begin incorporating those packages on a more regular and purposeful basis again. In addition to the offensive element, Gilliam’s return also might have a positive impact on the Patriots’ special teams operation. His leadership has been praised repeatedly by coordinator Jeremy Springer, while he also might resume the three-unit role he played prior to his stint on IR: he was used on kickoff coverage, kickoff return and punt coverage, playing 41% of kicking game snaps over the first four weeks of the season. The kickoff coverage element in particular will be worth watching after the Patriots have had multiple breakdowns over the last few weeks. Adding as experienced a special teamer as Gilliam to the mix might help fix those issues. OL Greg Van Roten: Activated to 53-man roster We know that the Patriots offensive line is going to look different compared to the one that started last Sunday’s game against the Packers. The only question is how different. Obviously, three spots are set in stone as they very much have been for the entire season: Will Campbell and Morgan Moses will be the starting tackles, with Jared Wilson at center. The guard positions, meanwhile, remain a revolving door. Before looking into the options for Sunday and further into the future, let’s set the scene by looking at which interior O-linemen are, and are not, available right now: 53-man roster (5): Ben Brown (77 | LG), Jared Wilson (55 | C), Matt Pryor (65 | RG), Greg Van Roten (70), Walter Rouse (72) Practice squad (2): Xavier Newman-Johnson (64), Andrew Rupcich (67) IR (2): Mike Onwenu (71), Alijah Vera-Tucker (75) Ben Brown, who started last week at left guard, will not be available on Sunday against the Lions because of the knee injury he suffered in Week 9. This creates an opening Van Roten might be asked to fill, despite the fact that he played just one non-preseason snap at the position over the last seven years; the last time he played left guard extensively, Tom Brady was still the quarterback in New England. The problem is that the alternatives are not overly attractive either, especially looking at the Lions game. Matt Pryor has limited LG experience as well, while moving him would introduce change at two spots within a unit whose success depends largely on the chemistry between its individual members. Walter Rouse, meanwhile, is questionable to play in the game after showing concussion symptoms coming out of last week’s game versus the Packers. And so, Van Roten might still be the best option after all. Long-term, however, the goal is to bring Alijah Vera-Tucker back into the mix; who will then start at right guard between Pryor, Van Roten or Brown is a question for another time.
