teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Nandomania is upon Raider Nation. By trading former starter Kirk Cousins for a third-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, the Las Vegas Raiders are turning to the top pick in the 2026 draft Fernando Mendoza at quarterback. The move from a 38-year-old veteran to the 23-year-old rookie marks a sizeable shift for the Silver & Black. “Our expectation is for him to lead the offense, to lead the operation, and to go play a game here Sunday and be the leader of the team, be the leader of the offense,” Las Vegas head coach Klint Kubiak said of Mendoza. “We have to prepare him and give him a lot of reps to get him comfortable. So, our expectation is for him to lead the offense.” Standing 6-foot-5 and 225 pounds, Mendoza brings NFL-size with a livelier arm and fresh legs with mobility to the quarterback position, as opposed to Cousins. But where the veteran has the rook beat is game experience. While Cousins may be a statue as a pocket passer, he did provide his younger counterpart an ideal mentor and sounding board. And Las Vegas is banking on the nine games Mendoza sat and watched Cousins operate provided a blueprint for the rookie to follow. And what an opponent for Mendoza to make his first start against: The Seattle Seahawks. “Like I said, this is a new experience. It’s great. It’s against a fantastic opponent. However, I have so much trust in the coaching staff, in the front office, and my teammates and the leaders of the team to go out there and best support everybody’s 1/11th, so we can do our job to the best ability.” While Seattle is quite shaky offensively — ranking 18th in points scored and 17th in yards gained under rookie offensive coordinator Brian Fleury — head coach and defensive play caller Mike Macdonald has the Seahawks defense as one of the top units in the NFL. #Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza shared a statement thanking Kirk Cousins and his family: “It would’ve been really easy for Kirk to be a little more dismissive. He had me with open arms and has taught me so many things. … He shared it with no restrictions or constraints.” 🥹 pic.twitter.com/rUhol5ChiB — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) November 11, 2026 If both Mendoza and Kubiak are to get the Raiders aerial attack on track this Sunday, they’ll have to do it against the Seahawks’ top-ranked passing defense which is ranked No. 1 in air yards allowed (1,396). Seattle is also allowing the fourth-least passing touchdowns (nine) and have racked up the sixth-most interceptions (eight). Both the Raiders quarterback and head coach are eager to meet the challenge head-on, though. “It is, yeah. And every week in the NFL is tough, and this is the best defense in the NFL,” Kubiak said when asked about Mendoza’s start against a top-tier Seahawks defense being invaluable. “And again, he’s got to go do his job and not worry about a whole lot else. Everybody does their 1/11th, and everyone around him elevates their play.” Notice that 1/11th that both Mendoza and Kubiak were quick to drop during their respective times at the podium during media availability this week leading up the Week 10 matchup with the Seahawks? Kubiak’s offense epitomizes the all-11 approach. Ranked eighth in the NFL in points scored (238) and 15th in yards gained (2,979), Las Vegas passing game is ranked fifth in air yards (2,337) and are third-best in touchdowns (20). The offensive line — which has showcased much better pass protection ability than run blocking — kept Cousins upright for those 20 touchdowns and the expectation is the group doing the same for Mendoza. The stronger arm talent the Indiana product brings to the table should pay dividends for Raiders pass catchers like tight end Brock Bowers (team-leading 48 receptions, 658 yards, and six touchdowns), fleet-footed wide receiver Tre Tucker (33 receptions for 529 yards and four touchdowns), and running back Ashton Jeanty (42 receptions for 371 yards and three touchdowns. Add tight end Michael Mayer (39 catches for 388 yards and a touchdown), and Mendoza has weaponary at his disposal. Seattle HC Mike Macdonald on Raiders Klint Kubiak from NFL Owner's Meeting #raiders #raidernation #LasVegasRaiders #nfl #lasvegasraidersonsi pic.twitter.com/8PBukAXDVe — Hondo Carpenter (@HondoCarpenter) March 30, 2026 Las Vegas’ ground game is in the pits, however, and is ranked dead-last in yards gained (642) and yards per carry average (2.9). Much of this is due to lack of trench dominance and opposing defenses loading the box with eight defenders knowing Cousins presents zero threat to scramble and take off with his legs. Perhaps the Mendoza dynamic changes that for Kubiak’s offense? “But, hey, go through your progression, and obviously if it’s not there, you’ve got to go run the football. And then when you’re running the football, how do you protect yourself so that you can get us to the next down, because we need you available for the whole season,” Kubiak said regarding Mendoza trusting his eyes, staying in the pocket, and run as a last resort rather than too quickly. “You’re not trying to sell out for a yard on first-and-10, so it’s an ongoing learning process. But that’s also why when you’re selecting men in the draft, you identify their instincts. I liked Fernando’s instincts in college, and it’s his first NFL game. So, we’re all going to see. But I’m excited for his opportunity and just for the whole offense to go play together.” We’re going to find out if Kubiak’s quarterback-whisperer ways can transfer to Mendoza as it has with Sam Darnold (during the Raiders head coach’s time as Seattle offensive coordinator last season) and Cousins. While this game features the debut of Mendoza and matching up against Macdonald’s defense, underneath all this is this simple item between the Raiders and Seahawks: Kubiak misses Macdonald’s defense (Las Vegas’ group is led by rookie defensive coordinator Rob Leonard and ranks dead last in points allowed (268) and yards yielded (3,469)) and Macdonald misses Kubiak’s offense. Quote of Note “Kirk has taught me a multitude of lessons, but two of the ones that stick out right now from your question is, number one, always being prepared and doing everything possible you can to prepare yourself to best serve your teammates, to best serve the organization. So you go out there Sunday, regardless of the result, no doubt in your mind that you did everything possible to give your team and teammates the best chance to perform and win. And second is to be yourself. He’s always told everybody on the team, and he was a great leader and captain on the team and really brought us together and had a lot of togetherness. So that’s something that I look to exemplify and take from his lessons.” —Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza on what lessons from former starter Kirk Cousins sticks out

INJURY CRISIS: Las Vegas Raiders Face Seahawks Without Sam Darnold, Quentin Nelson, BIG Impact
How does Seattle Seahawks’ offense look with Drew Lock at quarterback for Week 10 matchup against Las Vegas Raiders?
teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 10 features an old-school AFC West rivalry as the then-Oakland, now Las Vegas Raiders and Seattle Seahawks had plenty of noteworthy divisional battles in the ‘80s and ‘90s before the NFL’s realignment that pushed Seattle into the NFC. To preview this weekend’s matchup , Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Field Gulls, and John Gilbert was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Seahawks for Raider Nation. Q: Sam Darnold has already been ruled out, meaning Drew Lock will make his fourth appearance and third start this season. What’s the difference in the Seahawks’ offense with Lock at quarterback, and what’s the fanbase’s confidence level in him as the starter? A: In years past, the answer to this would hark back to Pete Carroll’s 2023 comments about Lock making a couple of boneheaded throws. But when Lock has played this season, he has done a phenomenal job protecting the football. Darnold has missed two full games and only played five snaps in the season opener against the New England Patriots. Yet in spite of that, he is tied with Matthew Stafford for the most interceptions thrown in the NFC. On the flip side, Lock has five touchdowns and no interceptions while starting twice and playing most of the game against the Patriots. Of course, both of Lock’s starts came against the Arizona Cardinals, and the Arizona defense has done a solid job helping opposing quarterbacks bolster their stat lines this season, so we’ll see what Lock can do against the Raiders. Q: Jaxon Smith-Njigba is coming off a season where he led the NFL with nearly 1,800 receiving yards and won Offensive Player of the Year. So far in 2026, he’s the first and currently only player to eclipse the 1,000-yard mark while averaging about 10 yards per game more than he did last year . What makes JSN such a tough cover? Any suggestions for how to keep him in check? A: JSN has simply become a monster. He’s a very smooth and fluid route runner, and at the foundation of his greatness is the simple fact that all of his route stems look the same, making it impossible for defensive backs to anticipate what is coming. Add in great hands, a phenomenal work ethic and the reality that he is far and away the most dangerous offensive weapon in the Seattle arsenal. It’s a recipe to continue to feed him the ball until defenses can find a way to slow him down. Teams have tried almost everything to slow JSN down, but a consistent weakness has not yet been found. Jamming him at the line doesn’t stop him. Bracketing doesn’t stop him. Whatever opponents do, he just continues to find ways to get open and keep the offense moving. Q: Seattle’s rushing attack ranks 18th in yards per game, 25th in yards per carry and 27th in EPA per rush, according to Sumer Sports . Are the issues as simple as the offense missing Klint Kubiak and Kenneth Walker III? Has adding Quenton Nelson helped at all? A: Losing Kenneth Walker III to the Chiefs in free agency certainly hurt. The two biggest things the Seattle run game has missed for most of the first half of the season were the explosiveness and the ball security that Walker brought to the table. Yes, he had a style that could be infuriating at times, as he had a tendency to try to bounce so many runs outside looking for the big play. But the simple fact is that he has the burst and speed to create an outsized number of explosive plays, even while consistently finishing in the bottom half of the league in success rate. During his four seasons in Seattle, Walker fumbled a total of three times on 821 regular-season rushing attempts, while his replacements (Jadarian Price, Emanuel Wilson and George Holani) have put the ball on the ground six times in 195 rushing attempts so far this season. With that said, Zach Charbonnet is back in the lineup after tearing his ACL in the 2025 postseason, and his presence has been an instant upgrade at the position. Charbonnet is never going to present the big-play threat that Walker brought to the field on every rushing attempt, but Charbonnet is a disciplined back who will follow his blocking, while providing solid pass protection from the backfield in passing situations. As for Quenton Nelson, so far the trade has produced more excitement and hype than on-field production. Nelson apparently suffered a minor knee injury before the trade and had a procedure to address the issue. As such, with the Seahawks enjoying a bye week after facing off against the Raiders, he likely won’t be back in action again until Week 12 against the San Francisco 49ers. Q: Imagine you’re Kubiak game-planning for Fernando Mendoza’s first start against the vaunted Seahawks’ defense. How would you attack the defense and give the rookie quarterback his best chance at having success? Keep in mind that the Raiders are one of the few teams that are worse at running the ball than the Seahawks are. A: Where Kubiak really seemed to excel in Seattle was creating tendencies, or the appearance of tendencies, and then in high-leverage situations making it look like the offense is following that tendency, only to break off for a big play. So, whatever tendencies the Raiders offense has put on tape through the first half of the season, I expect those tendencies to be thrown out the window at key times within the games as Kubiak looks for big plays. The reality is that while the Seahawks defense is great, so far in 2026 the Seahawks offense hasn’t shown to be on par with the 2025 group, and between conservative playcalling and Drew Lock battling oblique and elbow issues, it might only take a couple of big plays for the Raiders to play spoilers against the defending champs. Q: Between Leonard Williams, Byron Murphy II, Devon Witherspoon, Ernest Jones IV and Nick Emmanwori, Seattle’s defense is filled with studs. If you had to pick one to deem the biggest key or X-factor for the unit, who would it be and why? A: As cliché as it sounds, there is no one piece that makes the defense tick. What makes Mike Macdonald’s defenses so good is that all eleven players are on the same page, doing their jobs at a high level. All of the big names on defense play key roles, but as a whole the group has enough depth that a single missing piece doesn’t send things off the rails. With that all said, everything starts in the trenches. So if Williams and Murphy aren’t able to do their thing up front, it leaves the rest of the defense hanging.

teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images After trading starting quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a third-round pick ahead of Tuesday’s deadline, the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 10 game against the Seattle Seahawks will forever be known as Fernando Mendoza’s first regular-season start for the Raiders . Of course, that’s the primary focus of this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! A: I get that a lot of people feel like the Raiders didn’t get a big enough return for Cousins, and initially, I was surprised they didn’t get more, too. I felt like John Spytek could have at least gotten an escalator on the pick where, if the Vikings made the NFC Championship, Super Bowl or whatever with Cousins, the pick becomes a second-rounder. However, all of the reporting after the fact has been that Minnesota wasn’t willing to go higher than a third for Cousins. So, if he wasn’t going to be the starter in Las Vegas for much longer, at least Spytek managed to get a Top 100 pick from a player who wasn’t going to be on next year’s roster and probably wasn’t going to be contributing for much longer this year anyway. Why wouldn’t the Vikings budge? Well, this is the same organization that moved on from Cousins a few years ago because they felt like they’d never be able to make a deep playoff run with him. Now that he’s older and didn’t join the team until halfway through the season, I’d imagine the logic is similar. Essentially, Minnesota was willing to take a chance that the 38-year-old can salvage the campaign, but not at the cost of potentially jeopardizing the club’s future, and drew a line at the third-rounder. Q: Can you please help me understand just what this team is doing? Trading your starting QB sends a signal that you’re no longer competing; you’re rebuilding. If that is the case, why do you keep your best trade asset in Maxx Crosby, who could bring you higher-round draft picks? Many people feel like the Raiders won’t win another game and fear for Mendoza. A: To be honest, I don’t think my answer is going to be satisfactory for you. It’s never been a secret that this is a rebuild year for the Raiders. They put a heavy emphasis on getting younger in the offseason, and it was always clear that Kirk Cousins was a bridge-gap starter until Mendoza was ready to start. The Cousins trade doesn’t happen if John Spytek and Klint Kubiak don’t think the latter is true. Spytek even said that the organization feels it can still win in the second half of this season with the rookie behind center. As far as not trading Crosby, I can agree that it’d make sense to try and get picks for him. However, the coaching staff and front office seem to think what he brings as a leader is more valuable to the culture that Kubiak is trying to build than a couple of draft picks. Also, keeping Crosby ties back to Spytek and Kubiak thinking they can stay in the playoff hunt with Mendoza. Now, if that plan falls flat and the team struggles down the stretch, maybe the strategy changes in the offseason and they look to move Crosby for picks again. But right now, the team’s brass appears comfortable seeing how the rest of the campaign plays out with the No. 1 pick leading the charge. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images" data-portal-copyright="Getty Images" /> A: I think you’re on the right track here where Kubiak’s game plan is going to be to get the ball out of Mendoza’s hands quickly and give him some easy throws, especially early on. There might not be a worse defense to face for a quarterback’s first NFL start given how many certified dudes the Seahawks have and how confusing Mike Macdonald’s scheme is. So, I think we’ll see a good amount of predetermined throws via screens, RPOs and bootlegs to simplify the rookie’s reads and try to neutralize Seattle’s pass rush. And of course, if there’s ever a game for the rushing attack to finally hit its stride, it’s this one. A: If I’m Macdonald, I’m throwing the book at Mendoza by giving him a lot of pressure looks pre-snap and changing the picture post-snap. Basically, the strategy is to try to overwhelm and confuse the rookie as much as possible so that he starts thinking too much and either holds onto the ball too long or makes a mistake that leads to a turnover. That’s why I think Kubiak should start the game with the predetermined quick throws mentioned above. Take the thinking off Fernando’s plate initially and let him get into a rhythm to build some confidence before opening up the playbook later on. To use a cross-sport reference, it’d be like a jump shooter looking to get fouled early so he can get to the line and see a few balls go through the hoop before letting it rip from three. A: I just want to start by giving you a hard time about asking a “two-part question” when there are four questions in here, LOL! I think Brock Bowers was always expected to be the primary receiver, and the actual receivers were viewed as complementary pieces. Bowers is doing a pretty good job of filling that role, seeing as he’s putting up wide receiver numbers, ranking tied for 14th in receptions (48), 10th in yards (658) and tied for sixth in touchdowns (six) among all pass-catchers, not just tight ends. And that’s after missing two games. As long as he’s around, the ‘WR1’ issue is overblown, in my opinion. On top of that, I think Tre Tucker has been a solid No. 2 this season. He ranks in the top 25 of receivers in catches (33, tied for 25th), yards (529, 17th) and touchdowns (four, tied for 11th). It also wouldn’t be surprising to me if Tucker is even more productive with Mendoza, given the latter brings more arm strength to the table than Cousins did. Now, Tucker is an impending free agent, and it might make more sense to save money for Bowers’ extension. So, wide receiver might still be an offseason need this year, but it doesn’t need to be a top priority if the plan is to open up the checkbook for the “football robot from heaven”. With Bech, he’s never been a great separator and has always been more reliant on winning contested catches. That was the book on him coming out of TCU, and it has shown up during his limited playing time in the NFL so far. He was/is a decent route runner; he just isn’t a high-level athlete to explode out of cuts and generate a lot of separation. He can win by being physical at the top of the route, but that isn’t going to result in wide-open targets. However, Bech has only run 59 routes this season, per Pro Football Focus , and just 19 in the two games since he returned from injury. So it’s too small of a sample size for me to say definitively that’s been the issue this year. A: I’d like to see Jackson Powers-Johnson get a shot at left guard, but I don’t think it will happen. One of the frustrations I have with Kubiak is that he seems to be too loyal to Spencer Buford. The Athletic’s Sam Warren didn’t say that directly when he joined Marcus and me on Tape Don’t Lie a couple of weeks ago , but Warren did mention that the coaching staff thinks higher of Burford than what his perception is outside of the building. Also, I’m sure some people are tired of me saying this; I get the feeling JPJ won’t be on the roster after this season. Unless an injury happens where he gets put back into the lineup and plays well, I think it’ll be a similar situation to Tyree Wilson, where Powers-Johnson gets shopped and traded in the offseason. A: Let’s slow down here for a second. Marcus and I aren’t saying Mike Washington Jr. is a bust. Last week just highlighted that he isn’t ready to take over as the lead running back ahead of Ashton Jeanty, which has always been the expectation for the fourth-round pick. I talked about this a bunch in the offseason (and I’m pretty sure Marcus did, too); Washington is more of a complementary back who is a home-run hitter rather than a bell cow due to his lack of vision and shiftiness. The Jets game opened the door for MJW to potentially take over because he did a decent job of keeping the offense on schedule, but last week was a different story. Still, he can be a good second option behind Jeanty moving forward. The coaching staff, especially the head coach, should have input on who the team drafts. They’re the ones coaching the players after all, and ignoring their opinions is how friction gets created within the organization. The general manager should be the one making the final call, but his decision should be the result of a collaborative effort with the scouting staff’s and coaching staff’s opinions factored in. It’s pretty common for coaches and the front office to meet during the offseason and hash out what players they want to target in the draft. Q: How has Rob Leonard treated No. 1 receivers like Chris Olave and Garrett Wilson? Will he adjust his coverage scheme to Jaxon Smith-Njigba? (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images" data-portal-copyright="Getty Images" /> A: Against Olave, Leonard’s strategy was essentially to keep Olave in front of the secondary to prevent giving up explosive plays, since he and Tyler Shough connected on a handful of deep shots in the first two weeks of the season. So, the Raiders were willing to give up any short routes to Olave. He still ended up having over 100 yards, but there were no explosive plays. That game is his second-lowest average depth of target (ADOT) of the season at 9.3 yards, and he had his highest YAC total (32 yards) of the season, per PFF . That was a decent strategy because the Saints didn’t have another receiver who could threaten the Raiders downfield, and Olave didn’t burn the Raiders deep. Against Wilson, Leonard went with a similar strategy initially. However, the cornerbacks had their worst game of the season collectively. Darien Porter started the game with poor awareness in Cover 3, losing Wilson for a 31-yard catch. On top of that, Eric Stokes got cooked by Adonai Mitchell for the majority of the game, while Jermod McCoy was beaten deep a handful of times as well. In other words, Leonard’s strategy didn’t work in New York because of a lack of execution in the secondary, and the Jets had more than one pass catcher who could burn the defense. I’d imagine the approach this Sunday will be to bracket or double team JSN as much as possible. He’s too good after the catch that you can’t just take away the deep shots and give him what he wants underneath. Also, there are very few corners (maybe none) who can cover Smith-Njigba consistently throughout a game, and Vegas certainly don’t have someone who can do it with how the position group has been playing lately. The good news is Seattle doesn’t have another pass-catcher who really strikes fear in opposing defenses, similar to New Orleans. Cooper Kupp is still solid, but he’s well past his prime at this stage. The bad news is JSN lines up all over the place, which makes it difficult to double team him because the defense doesn’t know where he’ll line up until the offense breaks the huddle. Bracket coverage impacts the entire secondary because the defense is dedicating two defenders to one pass catcher. If the unit doesn’t know where that pass catcher is going to be, then they have to adjust on the fly, which can lead to coverage breaks. Also, Smith-Njigba is arguably the best receiver in the game right now and can beat bracket coverage anyway. Long story short, the Raiders are probably going to have a tough time keeping JSN in check on Sunday. Most defenses in the league do, where it’s just a matter of trying to limit his damage as much as possible. Q: Matt, rewatching the last 4 games, I noticed the Raiders are having a hard time keeping the edge and defending passes on the flat. When they blitz, they’re easy to spot and defend. How much of this is Leonard’s scheme, and how much is a lack of quality defensive players? It just seems players are not in good positions to properly defend the run. Also, in your opinion, will Leonard be back next year? A: The run defense is more of a personnel issue, in my opinion. Not having a defensive tackle who can reset the line of scrimmage and/or get penetration allows the offense to dictate where the ball goes instead of the defense forcing cutbacks. That makes the linebackers’ jobs more difficult because the running back has more options/rushing lanes available, so the backers can’t play fast and attack downhill. Also, there are plenty of plays where the defensive tackles are getting pushed into the second level. That’s a big reason why the Raiders are struggling to stop 12 and 13 personnel runs. Two- and three-tight-end formations mean the defense has to account for more gaps, so it’s harder for the coordinator to scheme up blitzes and run stunts because there are more options for where the ball can go. When you scheme something up against the run, you’re guessing at where the ball is going, and the likelihood of picking wrong increases when there are more gaps to account for. It should be an educated guess based on the offense’s tendacies, but it’s still a guess. As far as coverage goes, it’s a twofold answer. Yes, Leonard’s scheme has left the defense susceptible in the flats, especially when he blitzes. However, opposing offenses are only worried about Maxx Crosby as a pass rusher right now because no one else is winning one-on-one opportunities consistently. So, they’re sliding the protection to Crosby to set up double teams, or just chip blocking him, and no one else is taking advantage of the opportunity to force the offense to adjust. Malcolm Koonce had a good start to the season where he was beating backup-caliber tackles, but Koonce has cooled off against better competition. And the interior pass rush has been pretty much nonexistent all season. So, Leonard has to blitz or manufacture pressure to avoid giving quarterbacks all day in the pocket. That thins out the secondary and leaves the defense susceptible to getting beaten in coverage. However, I do think his play calling has been too predictable because offenses seem to constantly have answers when he does bring pressure. Will Rob Leonard get fired at the end of the year? I understand why Klint Kubiak hasn’t done that yet because of the personnel issues I mentioned above. But Kubiak can’t have a defense that ranks dead last in points per game and is getting scored on at a historic pace and not make a significant change in the offseason. Maybe that’s a massive personnel change instead of firing the coordinator, but it isn’t like Kubiak and Leonard have a long history together. Q: The Raiders have received very limited return on investment from their defensive free agency signings. Do you think paying big bucks for young players coming off their rookie deals is the right approach? Should they target a bunch of solid veterans on reasonable short-term deals? A: In my opinion, Spytek approached free agency last offseason the right way by targeting younger players who were coming off rookie contracts. When a team is rebuilding, older veterans on short-term contracts are the type of players a general manager should stay away from. If the team’s core is young and the organization isn’t expecting to be a contender right away, then older guys who are near the end of their prime and not going to be around long-term aren’t worth bringing in. Instead, the roster-building strategy should be to get as many young and talented players as possible so that they can grow together and develop into a contending team for several years to come. But that doesn’t come without growing pains, and that’s where the Raiders are at right now. Now, if they finish this season around the seven- to eight-win mark and just have a few holes to patch over to become a legitimate contender in 2027, that’s when Spytek should pivot toward older veterans on short-term contracts in free agency. So the strategy could flip this offseason, especially if Mendoza hits the ground running. But as far as this past spring goes, I think the Raiders went about it the right way even if the early returns are underwhelming. That’ll do it for this week’s mailbag.
